Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: LLM-VA: Resolving the Jailbreak-Overrefusal Trade-off via Vector Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we simultaneously address both jailbreak and over-refusal in safety-aligned LLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes?
papers.core_contribution: LLM-V A aligns answer vectors with benign vectors through closed-form weight updates to resolve the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.conclusion: LLM-V A effectively resolves the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off by aligning vectors, without requiring fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode answer decisions and safety assessments as nearly orthogonal vectors.
Aligning these vectors through closed-form weight updates simultaneously reduces jailbreak and over-refusal.
LLM-V A achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility.
The method automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning.
The method is effective across 12 LLMs from 5 model families.
papers.limitation:
Binary toxicity assumption (only benign vs. toxic), whereas real-world toxicity is nuanced and multi-dimensional.
Model scale: experiments cover models up to 14B parameters; effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+) remains to be validated.
Training data dependency: requires labeled benign/toxic samples for SVM training; data quality and representativeness affect performance.
Difficulty applying to LLMs with chain-of-thought reasoning due to computational expense and randomness in reasoning steps.
Model-specific tuning required for optimal iteration count and layer selection.
future_direction: Extending LLM-V A to multi-class or fine-grained toxicity classification.
Validating effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+).
Improving generalization to unseen datasets.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs suffer from two failure modes: jailbreak (answering harmful inputs) and over-refusal (declining benign queries). Existing vector steering methods adjust the magnitude of answer vectors, but this creates a fundamental trade-off -- reducing jailbreak increases over-refusal and vice versa. We identify the root cause: LLMs encode the decision to answer (answer vector $v_a$) and the judgment of input safety (benign vector $v_b$) as nearly orthogonal directions, treating them as independent processes. We propose LLM-VA, which aligns $v_a$ with $v_b$ through closed-form weight updates, making the model's willingness to answer causally dependent on its safety assessment -- without fine-tuning or architectural changes. Our method identifies vectors at each layer using SVMs, selects safety-relevant layers, and iteratively aligns vectors via minimum-norm weight modifications. Experiments on 12 LLMs demonstrate that LLM-VA achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility, and automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning. Code and models are available at https://hotbento.github.io/LLM-VA-Web/.

papers.title: Unlearning Traces the Influential Training Data of Language Models
papers.research_question: Identifying the training datasets that influence a language model’s outputs is essential for minimizing the generation of harmful content and enhancing its performance.
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents UnTrac and UnTrac-Inv, methods that use unlearning (gradient ascent) to trace the influence of training datasets on a model's predictions, achieving higher accuracy than existing influence functions.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning approaches (UnTrac and UnTrac-Inv) can effectively trace the influence of training datasets on language model predictions, offering a more accurate alternative to existing influence functions.
papers.key_findings:
UnTrac and UnTrac-Inv accurately estimate the influence of training datasets, correlating well with ground-truth leave-dataset-out influence.
The methods outperform existing influence functions (GradDot, GradCos, HIF, TracIn) in tracing the influence of pretraining datasets on harmful content generation.
UnTrac works robustly with preconditioned optimizers (e.g., Adam) and sufficient unlearning steps.
UnTrac-Inv is efficient for many training datasets but is sensitive to hyperparameters like batch size, learning rate, and number of steps.
papers.limitation:
Further empirical investigations are expected to verify the effectiveness of the methods in various settings and tasks.
The methods are not immediately applicable in practical use without validation against leave-dataset-out, which is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Investigating the effectiveness of the methods with even larger models.
Using the methods to reveal the source of LLM's emergent abilities, such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Identifying the training datasets that influence a language model's outputs is essential for minimizing the generation of harmful content and enhancing its performance. Ideally, we can measure the influence of each dataset by removing it from training; however, it is prohibitively expensive to retrain a model multiple times. This paper presents UnTrac: unlearning traces the influence of a training dataset on the model's performance. UnTrac is extremely simple; each training dataset is unlearned by gradient ascent, and we evaluate how much the model's predictions change after unlearning. Furthermore, we propose a more scalable approach, UnTrac-Inv, which unlearns a test dataset and evaluates the unlearned model on training datasets. UnTrac-Inv resembles UnTrac, while being efficient for massive training datasets. In the experiments, we examine if our methods can assess the influence of pretraining datasets on generating toxic, biased, and untruthful content. Our methods estimate their influence much more accurately than existing methods while requiring neither excessive memory space nor multiple checkpoints.

papers.title: Aligned Probing: Relating Toxic Behavior and Model Internals
papers.research_question: How do LMs encode information about toxicity, and what is the interplay between their internals and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces aligned probing, a framework to relate model behavior and internals for toxicity, and shows that LMs encode toxicity information strongly in lower layers, and that stronger encoding of input toxicity leads to less toxic output.
papers.conclusion: Aligned probing traces text properties from input to output, revealing that model behavior heavily relies on input toxicity, highlighting a dilemma: generating semantically relevant output without inheriting unwanted properties like toxicity.
papers.key_findings:
LMs encode information about toxicity strongly in lower layers.
LMs replicate and amplify toxicity more than humans, especially for attributes sensitive to single words.
Instruction-tuned models are less toxic and encode toxicity differently, with information more spread across layers.
Less toxic models encode more information about input toxicity.
Causal interventions show that skipping layers increases toxicity, indicating that information about input toxicity helps generate less toxic text.
papers.limitation:
Classifying toxicity is non-trivial due to conceptual variations, dataset differences, and contextual nature.
Generalization is limited to English and specific model families.
Computational costs for probing and interventions are high.
future_direction: Apply aligned probing to analyze other aspects of generation, like stereotypical formulations.
Examine the nature of other mitigation methods, such as model merging.
papers.abstract: We introduce aligned probing, a novel interpretability framework that aligns the behavior of language models (LMs), based on their outputs, and their internal representations (internals). Using this framework, we examine over 20 OLMo, Llama, and Mistral models, bridging behavioral and internal perspectives for toxicity for the first time. Our results show that LMs strongly encode information about the toxicity level of inputs and subsequent outputs, particularly in lower layers. Focusing on how unique LMs differ offers both correlative and causal evidence that they generate less toxic output when strongly encoding information about the input toxicity. We also highlight the heterogeneity of toxicity, as model behavior and internals vary across unique attributes such as Threat. Finally, four case studies analyzing detoxification, multi-prompt evaluations, model quantization, and pre-training dynamics underline the practical impact of aligned probing with further concrete insights. Our findings contribute to a more holistic understanding of LMs, both within and beyond the context of toxicity.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: Reviving Your MNEME: Predicting The Side Effects of LLM Unlearning and Fine-Tuning via Sparse Model Diffing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically detect unintended side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned large language models without access to fine-tuning data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MNEME, a framework that uses sparse model diffing to detect unintended side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned LLMs without access to fine-tuning data, achieving high accuracy across multiple scenarios.
papers.conclusion: MNEME is a general-purpose framework that effectively detects side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned LLMs using sparse model diffing, highlighting the promise of scalable, data-agnostic auditing tools.
papers.key_findings:
MNEME achieves up to 95% accuracy in predicting side effects on WMDP unlearning tasks.
On emergent misalignment, MNEME achieves 68.2% accuracy with perfect precision.
In benign fine-tuning scenarios, MNEME shows strong performance with up to 92.9% accuracy.
Sparse model diffing effectively isolates behavioral shifts without requiring fine-tuning data.
Retraining on high-activation samples can partially reverse the detected side effects.
papers.limitation:
Relies on task-agnostic corpora which may not reflect specific fine-tuning distributions.
Interpretability pipeline depends on LLM-generated descriptions, which may introduce noise or imprecision.
Cross-Coder was not originally designed for model diffing, and architectural constraints may limit fine-grained change capture.
Provides correlational insights rather than causal guarantees.
Computationally demanding due to need for model activations and large-scale inference.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are frequently fine-tuned or unlearned to adapt to new tasks or eliminate undesirable behaviors. While existing evaluation methods assess performance after such interventions, there remains no general approach for detecting unintended side effects, such as unlearning biology content degrading performance on chemistry tasks, particularly when these effects are unpredictable or emergent. To address this issue, we introduce MNEME, Model diffiNg for Evaluating Mechanistic Effects, a lightweight framework for identifying these side effects using sparse model diffing. MNEME compares base and fine-tuned models on task-agnostic data (for example, The Pile, LMSYS-Chat-1M) without access to fine-tuning data to isolate behavioral shifts. Applied to five LLMs across three scenarios: WMDP knowledge unlearning, emergent misalignment, and benign fine-tuning, MNEME achieves up to 95 percent accuracy in predicting side effects, aligning with known benchmarks and requiring no custom heuristics. Furthermore, we show that retraining on high-activation samples can partially reverse these effects. Our results demonstrate that sparse probing and diffing offer a scalable and automated lens into fine-tuning-induced model changes, providing practical tools for understanding and managing LLM behavior.

papers.title: Neuroplasticity and Corruption in Model Mechanisms: A Case Study Of Indirect Object Identification
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning on corrupted data affect model mechanisms, and how does retraining on clean data recover them?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning amplifies existing model mechanisms, corruption localizes to specific circuit components, and models exhibit neuroplasticity by relearning original mechanisms when retrained on clean data.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals how fine-tuning and corruption affect model mechanisms, and models exhibit inherent inertia allowing recovery of original mechanisms, highlighting the importance of interpretability for understanding model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific fine-tuning leads to Circuit Amplification, where existing circuit components are enhanced and new components replicating prior mechanisms emerge.
Toxic fine-tuning corrupts model mechanisms by altering specific attention heads in the circuit, rather than introducing new mechanisms.
Models show neuroplasticity: retraining corrupted models on clean data quickly recovers original mechanisms, often with amplification.
Amplification involves increased capacity of attention heads, seen in higher logit attribution and changed attention patterns.
Corruption mechanisms differ between datasets: Name Moving affects Name Mover and S-Inhibition heads, while Subject Duplication alters Name Mover and Negative Name Mover heads.
future_direction: Exploring more defined attacks through fine-tuning.
Investigating the 'twinning' behavior of Name Mover and Negative Name Mover heads in other tasks.
Further explorations to justify robustness to Duplication corruption.
papers.abstract: Previous research has shown that fine-tuning language models on general tasks enhance their underlying mechanisms.However, the impact of fine-tuning on poisoned data and the resulting changes in these mechanisms are poorly understood.This study investigates the changes in a model's mechanisms during toxic finetuning and identifies the primary corruption mechanisms.We also analyze the changes after retraining a corrupted model on the original dataset and observe neuroplasticity behaviors, where the model relearns original mechanisms after fine-tuning the corrupted model.Our findings indicate that: (i) Underlying mechanisms are amplified across task-specific fine-tuning which can be generalized to longer epochs, (ii) Model corruption via toxic fine-tuning is localized to specific circuit components, (iii) Models exhibit neuroplasticity when retraining corrupted models on clean dataset, reforming the original model mechanisms.

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: Anchoring Refusal Direction: Mitigating Safety Risks in Tuning via Projection Constraint
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate safety risks posed by Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) while preserving task performance gains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a projection-constraint method (ProCon) that stabilizes the refusal direction in LLM hidden states during instruction fine-tuning, effectively mitigating associated safety risks without compromising task performance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that anchoring the refusal direction via a projection constraint method effectively mitigates safety risks introduced by instruction fine-tuning, providing an interpretability-driven approach for safer LLM tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal direction (r-direction), a key representation for safety, drifts during instruction fine-tuning, which is identified as a primary cause of emerging safety risks.
Applying a projection constraint on hidden states along the r-direction can mitigate this drift and reduce safety risks.
A warm-up strategy that applies strong constraints in early training stages and broadening the data distribution with safety-oriented samples further enhances the method's effectiveness and stability.
The proposed ProCon method, especially the enhanced ProCon_wu_safe variant, consistently outperforms strong baselines in mitigating safety risks across various LLMs and scenarios while preserving task performance.
papers.abstract: Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) has been widely adopted as an effective post-training strategy to enhance various abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, prior studies have shown that IFT can significantly compromise LLMs' safety, particularly their ability to refuse malicious instructions, raising significant concerns. Recent research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs has identified the refusal direction (r-direction) in the hidden states, which plays a pivotal role in governing refusal behavior. Building on this insight, our study reveals that the r-direction tends to drift during training, which we identify as one of the causes of the associated safety risks. To mitigate such drift, our proposed ProCon method introduces a projection-constrained loss term that regularizes the projection magnitude of each training sample's hidden state onto the r-direction. Our initial analysis shows that applying an appropriate constraint can effectively mitigate the refusal direction drift and associated safety risks, but remains limited by overall performance barriers. To overcome this barrier, informed by our observation of early-stage sharp drift and a data-driven perspective, we introduce a warm-up strategy that emphasizes early-stage strong constraints and broaden the data distribution to strengthen constraint signals, leading to an enhanced ProCon method. Experimental results under various datasets, scenarios, and LLMs demonstrate that our method can significantly mitigate safety risks posed by IFT while preserving task performance gains. Even compared with strong baselines, our method consistently delivers superior overall performance. Crucially, our analysis indicates that ProCon can contribute to stabilizing the r-direction during training, while such an interpretability-driven exploration of LLMs' internal mechanisms lays a solid foundation for future safety research.

papers.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does anchoring bias in LLMs reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts in internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Integrates log-probability-based behavioral analysis with exact Shapley-value attribution to measure anchoring bias in LLMs, introducing an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score.
papers.conclusion: Anchoring bias in LLMs is robust and quantifiable, with implications for using LLMs as decision systems and for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Robust anchoring effects are observed in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution showing that anchors influence reweighting.
Smaller models like GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability in anchoring sensitivity, suggesting scale may modulate effects.
Attributional effects vary across prompt designs, indicating fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes.
The Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) ranks models based on combined behavioral and attributional evidence.
Behavioral anchoring is consistent across models, but attribution alignment can be discordant, especially in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Discretization of outputs to fixed numeric strings
No mechanistic claims as internal parameters and circuits were not probed
Method only works for models with open log-probabilities of outputs
future_direction: Expanding to a broader set of models
Integrating attributional evidence with concept-based and mechanistic interpretability
Extending the methodology to other cognitive biases
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly examined as both behavioral subjects and decision systems, yet it remains unclear whether observed cognitive biases reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, offers a critical test case. While prior work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring, most evidence relies on surface-level outputs, leaving internal mechanisms and attributional contributions unexplored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis showing that anchors shift entire output distributions, with controls for training-data contamination; (2) exact Shapley-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor influence on model log-probabilities; and (3) a unified Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal robust anchoring effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution signaling that the anchors influence reweighting. Smaller models such as GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability, suggesting scale may modulate sensitivity. Attributional effects, however, vary across prompt designs, underscoring fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes. The findings demonstrate that anchoring bias in LLMs is robust, measurable, and interpretable, while highlighting risks in applied domains. More broadly, the framework bridges behavioral science, LLM safety, and interpretability, offering a reproducible path for evaluating other cognitive biases in LLMs.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: Internal Causal Mechanisms Robustly Predict Language Model Out-of-Distribution Behaviors
papers.research_question: Can internal causal mechanisms be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples?
papers.core_contribution: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and the paper proposes two methods (counterfactual simulation and value probing) that outperform causal-agnostic approaches.
papers.conclusion: Internal causal features are the most robust features for predicting output correctness under distribution shifts, and causal analysis of language models is not only explanatory but also predictive, contributing to reliability and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Internal causal mechanisms can be used to predict model out-of-distribution behaviors.
Counterfactual simulation and value probing achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings.
Causal features are more robust than non-causal ones under distribution shifts.
papers.limitation:
The linearity assumption embedded in the chosen localization method may not hold for non-linear representations.
Reliance on prior knowledge to propose high-level causal models.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research now offers a variety of techniques for identifying abstract internal mechanisms in neural networks. Can such techniques be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples? In this work, we provide a positive answer to this question. Through a diverse set of language modeling tasks--including symbol manipulation, knowledge retrieval, and instruction following--we show that the most robust features for correctness prediction are those that play a distinctive causal role in the model's behavior. Specifically, we propose two methods that leverage causal mechanisms to predict the correctness of model outputs: counterfactual simulation (checking whether key causal variables are realized) and value probing (using the values of those variables to make predictions). Both achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform methods that rely on causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings, where predicting model behaviors is more crucial. Our work thus highlights a novel and significant application for internal causal analysis of language models.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models: Geometric Predictors and the Limits of Linear Approximations
papers.research_question: What are the underlying factors in model activation patterns that contribute to the observed variability in CAA steering vector reliability across different datasets and target behaviors? Can the training process of CAA steering vectors be modified to produce more consistently reliable control over language model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis demonstrates that steering vector unreliability is caused by a mismatch between the simple linear function class of CAA and the often non-linear latent target behavior representations. It identifies geometric predictors (directional agreement and separability) of steering reliability.
papers.conclusion: The reliability of CAA steering vectors is predictable from the geometry of the training activations. High directional agreement and clear separability along the difference-of-means line are key indicators of steerability.
papers.key_findings:
Higher cosine similarity (directional agreement) between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering.
Better separability of positive and negative activations along the steering direction predicts more reliable steering.
Steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct but perform similarly and have correlated efficacy across datasets.
Steering vector unreliability stems from the linear function class being too restrictive to approximate non-linear latent behavior representations.
Prompt types that leverage in-context learning (e.g., instructions, few-shot) lead to higher directional agreement and faster steering vector convergence.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to one model (Llama 2-7B-Chat) and one family of steering methods (CAA).
The analysis is restricted to binary classification tasks and may not generalize to more complex behaviors.
The study does not investigate the impact of model scale or architecture.
future_direction: Developing more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.
Extending the analysis to more models, architectures, and a broader range of behaviors.
Investigating the impact of model scale on steering reliability.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method for controlling language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although effective on average, steering effect sizes vary across samples and are unreliable for many target behaviors. In my thesis, I investigate why steering reliability differs across behaviors and how it is impacted by steering vector training data. First, I find that higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering. Second, I observe that behavior datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated along the steering direction are more reliably steerable. Finally, steering vectors trained on different prompt variations are directionally distinct, yet perform similarly well and exhibit correlated efficacy across datasets. My findings suggest that steering vectors are unreliable when the latent target behavior representation is not effectively approximated by the linear steering direction. Taken together, these insights offer a practical diagnostic for steering unreliability and motivate the development of more robust steering methods that explicitly account for non-linear latent behavior representations.

papers.title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify directions in activation space (persona vectors) underlying personality traits in language models, and use them to monitor and control persona shifts during deployment and finetuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an automated pipeline to extract persona vectors from natural language descriptions, and demonstrates that these vectors can be used to monitor and control persona shifts in language models during deployment and finetuning.
papers.conclusion: Persona vectors provide a powerful framework for understanding and controlling personality shifts in large language models, with applications in monitoring, mitigation, and prevention of undesirable trait expression.
papers.key_findings:
Persona vectors can be extracted automatically and used to control trait expression via steering and to monitor prompt-induced behavioral shifts.
Finetuning-induced persona shifts are strongly correlated with activation changes along the corresponding persona vectors.
Post-hoc steering can mitigate unwanted persona shifts after finetuning, but may degrade general capabilities.
Preventative steering during finetuning can limit persona shifts while better preserving general capabilities.
Projection of training data onto persona vectors can predict persona shifts before finetuning, enabling data filtering.
papers.limitation:
Persona vectors are effective for detecting clear prompt-induced shifts but may be less reliable for more subtle behavioral changes in deployment settings.
Steering interventions can introduce side effects and degrade model performance on general capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models interact with users through a simulated 'Assistant' persona. While the Assistant is typically trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, it sometimes deviates from these ideals. In this paper, we identify directions in the model's activation space-persona vectors-underlying several traits, such as evil, sycophancy, and propensity to hallucinate. We confirm that these vectors can be used to monitor fluctuations in the Assistant's personality at deployment time. We then apply persona vectors to predict and control personality shifts that occur during training. We find that both intended and unintended personality changes after finetuning are strongly correlated with shifts along the relevant persona vectors. These shifts can be mitigated through post-hoc intervention, or avoided in the first place with a new preventative steering method. Moreover, persona vectors can be used to flag training data that will produce undesirable personality changes, both at the dataset level and the individual sample level. Our method for extracting persona vectors is automated and can be applied to any personality trait of interest, given only a natural-language description.

papers.title: What Can We Actually Steer? A Multi-Behavior Study of Activation Control
papers.research_question: How does activation steering effectiveness vary across different behavior types, and can the nature of target behaviors predict steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with internal traits like personality and misalignment being more steerable than knowledge-dependent behaviors, and vector separation does not predict success.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is not a universal control method but a semantic modulator effective for abstract, internal dispositions but ineffective for knowledge-heavy roleplay or precise formatting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Steering effectiveness bifurcates between internal traits (e.g., personality, misalignment) and external knowledge (e.g., public figures), with internal traits being more steerable.
Trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with steering coefficient strength, peaking at moderate coefficients while coherence and relevance decline monotonically.
Vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, contradicting the intuition that larger activation differences yield better control.
Larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering without coherence collapse, improving steering quality despite smaller raw activation differences.
Misalignment behaviors such as hallucination and sycophancy are highly steerable, indicating potential safety risks where adversarial actors could easily amplify harmful traits.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily used Llama 3.1 8B, and steerability may scale non-linearly with model size.
Steering was restricted to Layer 15, and different behaviors might be localized at different layers.
Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) for evaluation introduces potential biases in scoring.
future_direction: Future work should explore whether more sophisticated vector diagnostics or non-linear relationships might better predict steerability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require precise behavior control for safe and effective deployment across diverse applications. Activation steering offers a promising approach for LLMs' behavioral control. We focus on the question of how steering effectiveness varies across different behavior types and whether the nature of target behaviors can predict steering success. We address this through empirical analysis of activation steering across 50 behaviors that span persona archetypes, personality traits, misalignment behaviors, style cues, and impersonation of public figures. We present a set of comprehensive experiments on coefficient optimization, vector properties, and data requirements to provide comprehensive guidance for the implementation of activation steering. Our analysis demonstrates that steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with different behavioral categories exhibiting distinct response patterns to intervention strength. We find that trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with a steering coefficient strength. We also show that vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, but larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering. These findings provide empirically grounded guidance for implementing activation steering and demonstrate that steering effectiveness is heavily influenced by behavior type.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Linear Personality Probing and Steering in LLMs: A Big Five Study
papers.research_question: Whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior in large language models.
papers.core_contribution: Linear directions aligned with Big Five traits are effective for personality probing, but steering is context-dependent, working well in forced-choice tasks but limited in open-ended generation or when prompt context is present.
papers.conclusion: Personality-related signals are embedded in the model's representational geometry, but steering vectors show strong context-dependency and are easily overridden by prompt context.
papers.key_findings:
Linear directions derived from regression align with Big Five traits and generalize to trait-relevant adjectives.
Steering with these vectors reliably shifts responses in forced-choice personality assessments.
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering has minimal effect in open-ended generation tasks.
Regression-derived directions are more effective than SVD-derived directions for steering.
papers.limitation:
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering is difficult to measure in open-ended generation where clear evaluation metrics are unavailable.
Aggregation across items and characters may obscure personality signals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit distinct and consistent personalities that greatly impact trust and engagement. While this means that personality frameworks would be highly valuable tools to characterize and control LLMs' behavior, current approaches remain either costly (post-training) or brittle (prompt engineering). Probing and steering via linear directions has recently emerged as a cheap and efficient alternative. In this paper, we investigate whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior. Using Llama 3.3 70B, we generate descriptions of 406 fictional characters and their Big Five trait scores. We then prompt the model with these descriptions and questions from the Alpaca questionnaire, allowing us to sample hidden activations that vary along personality traits in known, quantifiable ways. Using linear regression, we learn a set of per-layer directions in activation space, and test their effectiveness for probing and steering model behavior. Our results suggest that linear directions aligned with trait-scores are effective probes for personality detection, while their steering capabilities strongly depend on context, producing reliable effects in forced-choice tasks but limited influence in open-ended generation or when additional context is present in the prompt.

papers.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning
papers.research_question: How can refusal behavior in safety-aligned language models be ablated without causing collateral damage to core capabilities like math and coding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), a method that cleans refusal vectors by orthogonalizing against capability and style directions, enabling precise ablation of refusal behavior with minimal distribution drift and preserved capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SRA treats refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem, achieving behavioral editing with dramatically reduced drift and preserved capabilities compared to standard methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on wikitext_2_raw and minimal distribution drift.
Standard ablation induces severe distribution drift, while SRA maintains original distribution while achieving low refusal rates.
SRA preserves or improves math and code perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP datasets.
The dirty refusal vector is polysemantic, entangling refusal signals with unrelated linguistic structure and capability circuits.
Cleaning the vector via spectral residualization reduces 'Ghost Noise' damage caused by standard ablation.
papers.limitation:
The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction.
Evaluation limitations include refusal detection being definition-dependent, finite harmful prompt suites, and proxy drift metrics not substituting for comprehensive behavioral evaluation.
future_direction: Automating atom discovery or expanding registries to handle unseen confounds.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models systematically refuse harmful requests. While activation steering can modulate refusal, ablating the raw "refusal vector" calculated from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts often causes collateral damage and distribution drift. We argue this degradation occurs because the raw vector is polysemantic, entangling the refusal signal with core capability circuits and linguistic style. We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA) to distill these steering directions. SRA constructs a registry of independent Concept Atoms representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, then uses ridge-regularized spectral residualization to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a clean refusal direction that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model's semantic geometry. Across five models (Qwen3-VL and Ministral series), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0-2%) with negligible perplexity impact on Wikitext-2 (mean delta PPL approx. 0.02) and minimal distribution drift. Notably, standard ablation on Qwen3-VL-4B induces severe drift (first-token KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate. Using teacher-forced perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP as a high-resolution capability proxy, we show SRA preserves math and code distributions. These results suggest that common "model damage" is often "Ghost Noise," defined as the spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we balance safety and utility in large language models against jailbreak attacks by adjusting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Jailbreak Antidote, a method for real-time safety-utility balance by sparsely adjusting internal states during inference, showing that safety information is sparsely distributed and adjusting approximately 5% of the state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution for real-time safety adjustments in LLMs by directly manipulating internal states, enhancing safety while preserving utility and opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
Jailbreak Antidote achieves high defense success rates (DSR) across nine LLMs and ten jailbreak attack methods.
The method preserves model utility, maintaining high Win Rates on AlpacaEval while enhancing safety.
The approach is efficient, introducing negligible computational overhead and no additional token cost during inference.
The safety direction can be identified via PCA on hidden states from benign and harmful prompts.
papers.limitation:
The method requires pre-defined scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k; dynamically adapting these based on context or model confidence could improve flexibility.
Smaller models are inherently limited by their reduced parameter space, which may restrict the extent of safety adjustment.
Developing robust mechanisms to counter adversaries capable of explicitly exploiting the adjustments in internal states remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Dynamically adapting the scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k based on context or model confidence.
Addressing extreme adversarial settings where attackers explicitly exploit the internal state adjustments.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other aspects of model alignment, such as fairness or domain adaptation.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks, which manipulate LLMs into generating harmful content, pose significant challenges to this balance. Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: From Language Modeling to Instruction Following: Understanding the Behavior Shift in LLMs after Instruction Tuning
papers.research_question: How does instruction tuning change the internal mechanisms of LLMs to enable instruction following, specifically in terms of prompt-response attribution, self-attention patterns, and feed-forward network concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides an internal perspective on how instruction tuning enables instruction following by making models recognize instruction words, self-attention heads focus on instruction verbs, and feed-forward networks adapt knowledge to user-oriented tasks.
papers.conclusion: These insights contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of instruction tuning and lay the groundwork for future work that aims at explaining and optimizing LLMs for various applications.
papers.key_findings:
Instruction tuning enables models to recognize instruction words in user prompts and drives the generation process to be consistently conditioned on these words.
Instruction tuning encourages self-attention heads to learn more word relations with instruction verbs than common verbs, especially in lower and middle layers.
Instruction tuning adapts the pre-trained knowledge encoded by feed-forward networks into user-oriented tasks without changing their linguistic structures, effectively rotating the basis of their representation space.
papers.limitation: The importance density method lacks positional awareness and can be fooled by repetitive responses, which may not accurately reflect the model's internal behaviors in some cases.
future_direction: Address the positional awareness shortcoming in the importance density method or integrate a step to identify and handle repetitive responses.
Apply the toolbox to understand LLMs for various other purposes beyond instruction tuning.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success, where instruction tuning is the critical step in aligning LLMs with user intentions. In this work, we investigate how the instruction tuning adjusts pre-trained models with a focus on intrinsic changes. Specifically, we first develop several local and global explanation methods, including a gradient-based method for input-output attribution, and techniques for interpreting patterns and concepts in self-attention and feed-forward layers. The impact of instruction tuning is then studied by comparing the explanations derived from the pre-trained and instruction-tuned models. This approach provides an internal perspective of the model shifts on a human-comprehensible level. Our findings reveal three significant impacts of instruction tuning: 1) It empowers LLMs to recognize the instruction parts of user prompts, and promotes the response generation constantly conditioned on the instructions. 2) It encourages the self-attention heads to capture more word-word relationships about instruction verbs. 3) It encourages the feed-forward networks to rotate their pre-trained knowledge toward user-oriented tasks. These insights contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of instruction tuning and lay the groundwork for future work that aims at explaining and optimizing LLMs for various applications. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/JacksonWuxs/Interpret_Instruction_Tuning_LLMs.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
