Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: NeST: Neuron Selective Tuning for LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we achieve efficient and effective safety alignment in large language models by selectively tuning safety-relevant neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons by clustering them and applying shared updates, achieving strong safety performance with extreme parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: NeST provides a practical, efficient, and effective method for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling targeted adaptation of safety behavior with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
NeST reduces the average attack success rate from 44.5% to 4.36%, a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations.
NeST requires only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average, a 17,310× decrease compared to full fine-tuning and 9.25× reduction relative to LoRA.
NeST consistently achieves stronger safety performance than LoRA and Circuit Breaker across 10 open-weight LLMs.
NeST preserves core model capabilities on standard reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
NeST remains robust across diverse inference settings and input modalities, including text-only and multimodal generation.
papers.limitation: NeST relies on a safety-aligned base model and a diverse set of prompts for safety neuron detection, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending NeST to other model families and architectures.
Automating the selection of hyperparameters such as the number of clusters.
Applying NeST to other tasks beyond safety, such as task-specific adaptation.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is essential for the responsible deployment of large language models (LLMs). Yet, existing approaches often rely on heavyweight fine-tuning that is costly to update, audit, and maintain across model families. Full fine-tuning incurs substantial computational and storage overhead, while parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA trade efficiency for inconsistent safety gains and sensitivity to design choices. Safety intervention mechanisms such as circuit breakers reduce unsafe outputs without modifying model weights, but do not directly shape or preserve the internal representations that govern safety behavior. These limitations hinder rapid and reliable safety updates, particularly in settings where models evolve frequently or must adapt to new policies and domains. We present NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that strengthens refusal behavior by selectively adapting a small subset of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. NeST aligns parameter updates with the internal organization of safety behavior by clustering functionally coherent safety neurons and enforcing shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted and stable safety adaptation without broad model modification or inference-time overhead. We benchmark NeST against three dominant baselines: full fine-tuning, LoRA-based fine-tuning, and circuit breakers across 10 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes. Across all evaluated models, NeST reduces the attack success rate from an average of 44.5% to 4.36%, corresponding to a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations, while requiring only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average. This amounts to a 17,310x decrease in updated parameters compared to full fine-tuning and a 9.25x reduction relative to LoRA, while consistently achieving stronger safety performance for alignment.

papers.title: Do Personality Traits Interfere? Geometric Limitations of Steering in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether personality steering directions are geometrically independent in large language models, what happens to steering effectiveness when geometric independence is explicitly enforced, and if observed trait dependencies are consistent across different model families.
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering directions in LLMs are not geometrically independent; enforcing orthogonality does not eliminate cross-trait behavioral effects and can reduce steering strength and fluency, indicating that traits occupy a coupled subspace.
papers.conclusion: Personality traits in large language models are not independent directions in activation space, and geometric constraints on steering vectors have limitations in achieving fully independent trait control.
papers.key_findings:
Personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence, with steering one trait inducing changes in others.
Enforcing geometric independence through hard orthonormalisation does not eliminate cross-trait effects and reduces fluency.
Cross-trait dependencies are consistent across different model families like LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B.
Model-specific modulation exists, e.g., Neuroticism steering is strong in LLaMA-3 but weak in Mistral-8B.
Soft constraint methods like selective or soft projection offer a better trade-off between disentanglement and semantic preservation.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a small set of large language models and personality datasets.
Relies on linear geometric constraints; other orthogonalisation or projection methods are not explored.
Uses LLMs as judges for behavioral assessment without human evaluation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to a broader range of model families and trait representations.
Explore other orthogonalisation or projection methods beyond linear constraints.
Incorporate human evaluation or complementary metrics for assessment.
papers.abstract: Personality steering in large language models (LLMs) commonly relies on injecting trait-specific steering vectors, implicitly assuming that personality traits can be controlled independently. In this work, we examine whether this assumption holds by analysing the geometric relationships between Big Five personality steering directions. We study steering vectors extracted from two model families (LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B) and apply a range of geometric conditioning schemes, from unconstrained directions to soft and hard orthonormalisation. Our results show that personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence: steering one trait consistently induces changes in others, even when linear overlap is explicitly removed. While hard orthonormalisation enforces geometric independence, it does not eliminate cross-trait behavioural effects and can reduce steering strength. These findings suggest that personality traits in LLMs occupy a slightly coupled subspace, limiting fully independent trait control.

papers.title: Command-V: Pasting LLM Behaviors via Activation Profiles
papers.research_question: How can behaviors be efficiently transferred from one large language model to another without requiring fine-tuning or backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Command-V, a backpropagation-free method that transfers behaviors between LLMs by profiling layer activations, deriving linear converters, and applying donor adapter interventions in the recipient's activation space, matching fine-tuning performance with minimal compute.
papers.conclusion: Command-V provides an efficient, training-free method for behavior transfer across LLMs, pushing the Pareto frontier in cost and performance, with promising future directions for improvement and application.
papers.key_findings:
Command-V matches or exceeds direct fine-tuning performance on safety refusal, jailbreaking, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.
The method requires orders of magnitude less compute than fine-tuning and does not need the original training data.
Behaviors can be transferred across different model architectures, though effectiveness varies.
Transfer can sometimes lead to overrefusal or degraded instruction following, especially in smaller models.
Activation profiles built on a general prompt set (LIMA) are effective for transferring task-specific behaviors.
papers.limitation:
Command-V is not useful when the adapters have very little impact on the donor model to begin with.
Model utility can be compromised after applying Command-V, with recipient models sometimes failing to improve task performance or suffering from output collapse.
Architectural divergence between models reduces effectiveness for some behaviors like refusal enhancement and reasoning.
future_direction: Porting behaviors from high-resource to low-resource language models.
Task composition by pasting several specialist adapters into one generalist model.
Exploring non-linear converters or trained converters beyond the least-squares method.
papers.abstract: Retrofitting large language models (LLMs) with new behaviors typically requires full finetuning or distillation-costly steps that must be repeated for every architecture. In this work, we introduce Command-V, a backpropagation-free behavior transfer method that copies an existing residual activation adapter from a donor model and pastes its effect into a recipient model. Command-V profiles layer activations on a small prompt set, derives linear converters between corresponding layers, and applies the donor intervention in the recipient's activation space. This process does not require access to the original training data and needs minimal compute. In three case studies-safety-refusal enhancement, jailbreak facilitation, and automatic chain-of-thought reasoning--Command-V matches or exceeds the performance of direct finetuning while using orders of magnitude less compute. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/GithuBarry/Command-V/.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: Ability Transfer and Recovery via Modularized Parameters Localization
papers.research_question: How are abilities distributed within LLM parameters? The paper investigates this by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ACT, a method that localizes ability-relevant channels in LLMs via cross-model activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, enabling efficient ability transfer and recovery while minimizing interference.
papers.conclusion: ACT enables efficient and effective ability transfer and recovery by localizing and transferring modularized ability-relevant parameters, and it can integrate multiple abilities into a single model with minimal interference.
papers.key_findings:
Large activation differences are concentrated in a small fraction of channels (typically <5%).
Activation difference distributions across different layers exhibit consistent heavy-tailed patterns.
Ability-specific channels are naturally disentangled across different language-domain abilities.
Ability-specific channels exhibit consistency after fine-tuning across different fine-tuned variants.
Ability-specific channels selected by activations differ from largely updated ones during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes the availability of a base model and an ability model that share the same architecture and tokenizer, and are preferably derived from the same pretrained checkpoint.
The effectiveness of ACT may be limited when the parameter drift between the base and ability models is too large, as observed in some continuous pre-training scenarios.
future_direction: Extending ACT to more diverse abilities and tasks beyond reasoning domains.
Exploring the theoretical foundations of activation-based ability localization.
Applying ACT to other model families and architectures beyond transformers.
papers.abstract: Large language models can be continually pre-trained or fine-tuned to improve performance in specific domains, languages, or skills, but this specialization often degrades other capabilities and may cause catastrophic forgetting. We investigate how abilities are distributed within LLM parameters by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models. Across layers and modules, we find that ability-related activations are highly concentrated in a small set of channels (typically <5\%), and these channels are largely disentangled with good sufficiency and stability. Building on these observations, we propose ACT (Activation-Guided Channel-wise Ability Transfer), which localizes ability-relevant channels via activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, followed by lightweight fine-tuning for compatibility. Experiments on multilingual mathematical and scientific reasoning show that ACT can recover forgotten abilities while preserving retained skills. It can also merge multiple specialized models to integrate several abilities into a single model with minimal interference. Our code and data will be publicly released.

papers.title: Competence-Based Analysis of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand and measure the linguistic competence of large language models with respect to their representation and use of human-interpretable linguistic properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the CALM framework for analyzing LLM competence using causal probing and develops Gradient-Based Interventions (GBIs), a novel causal probing method that can target arbitrarily-encoded representations.
papers.conclusion: CALM and GBIs provide an effective framework and methodology for analyzing LLM competence, explaining behavioral patterns across lexical inference tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa are partially competent on lexical inference tasks, with BERT generally more competent than RoBERTa.
Competence scores correlate with task performance, providing an explanation for brittle performance under prompt variation.
Gradient-Based Interventions enable causal probing of a broader range of representations than prior techniques.
papers.limitation:
Gradient-Based Interventions face a tradeoff between completeness (manipulating the target property) and selectivity (avoiding damage to non-target properties).
Probes may leverage spurious information rather than the true representation of the target property.
Experiments are conducted on comparatively small, well-studied models (BERT and RoBERTa) and may not generalize to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Scaling CALM to larger, more powerful models and more difficult tasks.
Studying the impact of model training and fine-tuning choices on learned representations.
Using CALM for multitask learning and understanding task dependencies.
Combining CALM with causal graph discovery algorithms to infer implicit task representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent successes of large, pretrained neural language models (LLMs), comparatively little is known about the representations of linguistic structure they learn during pretraining, which can lead to unexpected behaviors in response to prompt variation or distribution shift. To better understand these models and behaviors, we introduce a general model analysis framework to study LLMs with respect to their representation and use of human-interpretable linguistic properties. Our framework, CALM (Competence-based Analysis of Language Models), is designed to investigate LLM competence in the context of specific tasks by intervening on models' internal representations of different linguistic properties using causal probing, and measuring models' alignment under these interventions with a given ground-truth causal model of the task. We also develop a new approach for performing causal probing interventions using gradient-based adversarial attacks, which can target a broader range of properties and representations than prior techniques. Finally, we carry out a case study of CALM using these interventions to analyze and compare LLM competence across a variety of lexical inference tasks, showing that CALM can be used to explain behaviors across these tasks.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-Correction in LLMs: Towards Explainable Prompting via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does intrinsic self-correction prompting act as representation steering along interpretable latent directions?
papers.core_contribution: Intrinsic self-correction in LLMs functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by alignment between prompt-induced shifts and steering vectors and causal verification via activation addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings link self-correction prompting to representation steering along interpretable latent directions, highlighting the role of interpretability methods in understanding prompt-driven LLM phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-induced shifts in self-correction align with steering vectors constructed from contrastive pairs.
Activation injection with steering vectors causally reproduces behavioral changes in toxicity.
Detoxification is effective even with weak prompts, while toxification requires strong prompts.
Most of the behavioral change occurs in the first self-correction round.
Alignment between shifts and vectors peaks in mid-to-late layers for some models.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to toxicity-related behaviors and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other prompt-driven phenomena such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic self-correction refers to the phenomenon where a language model refines its own outputs purely through prompting, without external feedback or parameter updates. While this approach improves performance across diverse tasks, its mechanism remains unclear. We show that intrinsic self-correction functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by both alignment analysis and activation interventions. To achieve this, we analyze intrinsic self-correction via the representation shift induced by prompting. In parallel, we construct interpretable latent directions with contrastive pairs and verify the causal effect of these directions via activation addition. Evaluating six open-source LLMs, our results demonstrate that prompt-induced representation shifts in text detoxification and text toxification consistently align with latent directions constructed from contrastive pairs. In detoxification, the shifts align with the non-toxic direction; in toxification, they align with the toxic direction. These findings suggest that representation steering is the mechanistic driver of intrinsic self-correction. Our analysis highlights that understanding model internals offers a direct route to analyzing the mechanisms of prompt-driven LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Steer2Edit: From Activation Steering to Component-Level Editing
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors be reinterpreted as diagnostic signals to reveal how a target behavior is distributed across model components, and can this information be used to selectively modify those components via weight editing to achieve better attribute-utility trade-offs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEER2EDIT, a training-free framework that converts activation steering vectors into component-level rank-1 weight edits, achieving more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs by selectively redistributing behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.conclusion: STEER2EDIT provides a principled, training-free framework for converting steering vectors into component-level weight edits, enabling precise behavioral control with favorable attribute-utility trade-offs and interpretable, architecture-preserving model modifications.
papers.key_findings:
STEER2EDIT consistently achieves superior attribute-utility trade-offs compared to activation steering: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average.
The method produces interpretable, sparse edits: safety and truthfulness control are mediated by a small subset of attention heads, while reasoning efficiency is governed by distributed MLP neuron edits.
The edits are closed-form, require no fine-tuning, and yield a standalone edited model that preserves the original architecture and standard forward pass.
Component importance scores (cosine similarity between steering vector and component output) and Elastic-Net regularization are critical for stable and sparse editing.
The framework provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing, translating steering signals into interpretable parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Steering methods influence Large Language Model behavior by identifying semantic directions in hidden representations, but are typically realized through inference-time activation interventions that apply a fixed, global modification to the model's internal states. While effective, such interventions often induce unfavorable attribute-utility trade-offs under strong control, as they ignore the fact that many behaviors are governed by a small and heterogeneous subset of model components. We propose Steer2Edit, a theoretically grounded, training-free framework that transforms steering vectors from inference-time control signals into diagnostic signals for component-level rank-1 weight editing. Instead of uniformly injecting a steering direction during generation, Steer2Edit selectively redistributes behavioral influence across individual attention heads and MLP neurons, yielding interpretable edits that preserve the standard forward pass and remain compatible with optimized parallel inference. Across safety alignment, hallucination mitigation, and reasoning efficiency, Steer2Edit consistently achieves more favorable attribute-utility trade-offs: at matched downstream performance, it improves safety by up to 17.2%, increases truthfulness by 9.8%, and reduces reasoning length by 12.2% on average. Overall, Steer2Edit provides a principled bridge between representation steering and weight editing by translating steering signals into interpretable, training-free parameter updates.

papers.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of safety alignment in large language models to latent perturbations, and can minor shifts in internal representations trigger unsafe responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental lack of local robustness in the latent representations of safety-aligned LLMs, introduces a probing method and attack (ASA) to exploit this, and proposes a defense (LAPT) that improves robustness without harming general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Current safety alignment methods lack local robustness in the internal representational space, and robust AI safety requires fortifying internal representations rather than just modifying input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Minor perturbations to hidden activations can successfully jailbreak safety-aligned LLMs, revealing shallow alignment.
The Activation Steering Attack (ASA) is an effective, lightweight jailbreak method that generalizes across models.
A gradient-based variant (ASAgrad) is even more effective by using harmful suffixes as targets.
Vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific 'fragile layers' within models.
Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training (LAPT) can enhance alignment robustness against such latent attacks while preserving general task performance.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is a key requirement for building reliable Artificial General Intelligence. Despite significant advances in safety alignment, we observe that minor latent shifts can still trigger unsafe responses in aligned models. We argue that this stems from the shallow nature of existing alignment methods, which focus on surface-level refusal behaviors without sufficiently altering internal representations. Consequently, small shifts in hidden activations can re-trigger harmful behaviors embedded in the latent space. To explore the robustness of safety alignment to latent perturbations, we introduce a probing method that measures the Negative Log-Likelihood of the original response generated by the model. This probe quantifies local sensitivity in the latent space, serving as a diagnostic tool for identifying vulnerable directions. Based on this signal, we construct effective jailbreak trajectories, giving rise to the Activation Steering Attack (ASA). More importantly, these insights offer a principled foundation for improving alignment robustness. To this end, we introduce Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training~(LAPT), a fine-tuning strategy that inject controlled perturbations into hidden representations during training. Experimental results highlight that LAPT strengthen alignment robustness without compromising general capabilities. Our findings reveal fundamental flaws in current alignment paradigms and call for representation-level training strategies that move beyond surface-level behavior supervision. Codes and results are available at https://github.com/Carol-gutianle/LatentSafety.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How and where does fine-tuning affect the representations of a pre-trained model, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to a change in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning changes model representations and probing accuracy, but these changes are not solely due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge and require careful interpretation, as improvements with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning leads to changes in probing accuracy, but these changes are not solely attributable to encoding or forgetting linguistic knowledge and should be interpreted carefully.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger in higher layers.
The impact of fine-tuning on probing accuracy varies across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling after fine-tuning are often due to changes in attention distribution rather than new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, suggesting linguistic knowledge may become less linearly accessible.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using the pre-trained model with mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Investigate whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it non-linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how fine-tuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while fine-tuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of fine-tuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to Decode Activations Into Natural Language
papers.research_question: How can we train a language model to decode activations into natural language answers to open-ended questions about those activations (LATENTQA), and how can this be used for reading and controlling model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LatentInterpretationTuning (LIT), a method to train a decoder LLM to answer open-ended questions about model activations (LATENTQA), and demonstrates its effectiveness for reading activations and controlling model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LATENTQA, enabled by LIT, provides a powerful framework for reading and controlling model activations with natural language, and scales well with data and model size.
papers.key_findings:
LIT achieves higher accuracy than GPT-4 and SelfIE in uncovering hidden system prompts.
LIT outperforms linear probing and Patchscope in relational knowledge extraction.
LIT is the only method that significantly reduces bias in the debiasing task.
LIT can steer models to exhibit unseen behaviors (e.g., Golden Gate Claude).
LIT benefits from scaling in dataset and model size.
future_direction: Training LATENTQA systems on additional types of data (e.g., hierarchical instruction-following) to unlock novel applications.
Scaling LATENTQA to larger datasets and models.
Using LATENTQA for evaluating instruction following in long-context scenarios.
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods seek to understand language model representations, yet the outputs of most such methods -- circuits, vectors, scalars -- are not immediately human-interpretable. In response, we introduce LatentQA, the task of answering open-ended questions about model activations in natural language. Towards solving LatentQA, we propose Latent Interpretation Tuning (LIT), which finetunes a decoder LLM on a dataset of activations and associated question-answer pairs, similar to how visual instruction tuning trains on question-answer pairs associated with images. We use the decoder for diverse reading applications, such as extracting relational knowledge from representations or uncovering system prompts governing model behavior. Our decoder also specifies a differentiable loss that we use to control models, such as debiasing models on stereotyped sentences and controlling the sentiment of generations. Finally, we extend LatentQA to reveal harmful model capabilities, such as generating recipes for bioweapons and code for hacking.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance. Additionally, we propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a last-layer activation amplification module and a few LoRA layers, outperforming full LoRA fine-tuning on reasoning benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters. Our code and data are publicly released.

papers.title: NLSR: Neuron-Level Safety Realignment of Large Language Models Against Harmful Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we restore the safety of large language models after harmful fine-tuning without requiring additional training, by focusing on neuron-level updates?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, neuron-level safety realignment framework that restores model safety by identifying and patching safety-critical neurons based on similarity differences before and after fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Neuron-level safety realignment is an effective, training-free approach to restore safety in LLMs after harmful fine-tuning, without disrupting the task-specific optimization process.
papers.key_findings:
NLSR effectively restores safety in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks while maintaining task-level accuracy.
Safety-critical neurons show noticeable similarity differences after fine-tuning, which can be corrected by transplanting neurons from a reference model.
Adaptive safety-critical layer pruning is necessary for identifying safety-compromised layers.
After safety pre-amplification, various safety neuron identification methods (Wanda, SNIP, and the proposed method) show high similarity in localizing safety-critical neurons.
The method is decoupled from the fine-tuning phase and requires no additional training.
papers.abstract: The emergence of finetuning-as-a-service has revealed a new vulnerability in large language models (LLMs). A mere handful of malicious data uploaded by users can subtly manipulate the finetuning process, resulting in an alignment-broken model. Existing methods to counteract fine-tuning attacks typically require substantial computational resources. Even with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA, gradient updates remain essential. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{N}euron-\textbf{L}evel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{R}ealignment (\textbf{NLSR}), a training-free framework that restores the safety of LLMs based on the similarity difference of safety-critical neurons before and after fine-tuning. The core of our framework is first to construct a safety reference model from an initially aligned model to amplify safety-related features in neurons. We then utilize this reference model to identify safety-critical neurons, which we prepare as patches. Finally, we selectively restore only those neurons that exhibit significant similarity differences by transplanting these prepared patches, thereby minimally altering the fine-tuned model. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant safety enhancements in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks, while greatly maintaining task-level accuracy. Our findings suggest regions of some safety-critical neurons show noticeable differences after fine-tuning, which can be effectively corrected by transplanting neurons from the reference model without requiring additional training. The code will be available at \url{https://github.com/xinykou/NLSR}

papers.title: Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection for Fine-Tuned Large Language Models without Retraining
papers.research_question: How to achieve robust safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and without retraining, while maintaining utility and allowing continual adaptation to emerging safety concerns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSCP, a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that identifies sparse safety-critical neurons via multi-level representations and applies safety-direction projections to suppress harmful outputs with minimal parameter changes, preserving utility and enabling continual adaptation.
papers.conclusion: MSCP effectively enhances safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and no retraining, enabling continual adaptation and preserving utility, highlighting the value of fine-grained model introspection for scalable safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
MSCP reduces harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter edits (e.g., 4.67% for Qwen) while preserving model utility.
MSCP achieves continual safety improvement across multiple risk dimensions, with decreasing parameter changes for new dimensions (e.g., 0.73% for Terrorism).
Ablation shows that safety layers at one-third model depth (layers 10-15) yield the best safety and utility balance.
papers.limitation: The ability to continual learning across more complex and diverse safety dimensions remains an area for further investigation.
papers.abstract: While fine-tuning services drive the rapid expansion of task capabilities in large language models (LLMs), they are often accompanied by the degradation and reorganization of safety-aligned representations, making models more prone to deviating from human preferences and exposing them to emerging jailbreak risks. Existing post-fine-tuning defense methods predominantly rely on single-scale safety correction mechanisms, which struggle to achieve a robust balance among safety, model utility, and continual adaptability. We propose Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection (MSCP), a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that implicitly aligns global and localized safety activations through coordinated multi-level representations to isolate sparse neuron clusters governing safety-sensitive behaviors. It then applies composable safety-direction projections without retraining, effectively suppressing harmful outputs under minimal parameter perturbations while preserving task performance and improving alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-tuned LLM models demonstrate that our method significantly reduce harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter modifications, while preserving the model's utility. Furthermore, we introduce a task-specific, multi-dimensional heterogeneous safety activation clustering mechanism that enables continual defense and generalization capability against unforeseen emerging safety concerns.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Local Contrastive Editing of Gender Stereotypes
papers.research_question: How can we localize individual weights that drive stereotypical gender bias in language models and modify these weights to steer and mitigate the bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces local contrastive editing, a two-step method to localize and edit a small subset (<0.5%) of model weights that encode gender bias, enabling flexible control and mitigation of bias while largely preserving model performance.
papers.conclusion: Stereotypical gender bias is encoded in specific subsets of weights within language models, and local contrastive editing can effectively identify and modify these subsets to control and mitigate bias.
papers.key_findings:
A very small subset (<0.5%) of model weights is responsible for encoding stereotypical gender bias.
Local contrastive editing strategies (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning) can successfully steer and mitigate gender bias in a controlled manner.
The identified bias-encoding weights are concentrated in higher layers of the transformer, particularly in the attention output dense layer.
Editing based on strategic localization is crucial; uninformed editing of random weights does not effectively change bias.
The method preserves the model's language modeling ability and downstream task performance, except for value-based pruning which degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted using a single model architecture (BERT) and a single type of bias (gender bias).
Computational constraints limit the scope of experiments, as iterative magnitude pruning requires substantial resources.
The study uses a binary specification of gender (male/female), which does not encompass the full gender spectrum.
future_direction: Explore application of local contrastive editing to other tasks and domains beyond gender bias.
papers.abstract: Stereotypical bias encoded in language models (LMs) poses a threat to safe language technology, yet our understanding of how bias manifests in the parameters of LMs remains incomplete. We introduce local contrastive editing that enables the localization and editing of a subset of weights in a target model in relation to a reference model. We deploy this approach to identify and modify subsets of weights that are associated with gender stereotypes in LMs. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that local contrastive editing can precisely localize and control a small subset (< 0.5%) of weights that encode gender bias. Our work (i) advances our understanding of how stereotypical biases can manifest in the parameter space of LMs and (ii) opens up new avenues for developing parameter-efficient strategies for controlling model properties in a contrastive manner.

papers.title: A Review of Developmental Interpretability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is developmental interpretability, and how does it help understand the formation and evolution of capabilities in Large Language Models during training?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes the field of developmental interpretability for LLMs, highlighting how understanding training dynamics can provide insights into capability formation and enhance AI safety.
papers.conclusion: Developmental interpretability reveals LLMs as dynamic systems with rich ontogeny, providing a proactive approach to AI safety by understanding capability formation during training.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form through composition of attention heads, enabling in-context learning.
Knowledge acquisition follows a biphasic pattern from formation to optimization.
Emergent abilities arise as phase transitions when pre-training loss crosses critical thresholds.
In-context learning can be transient and replaced by in-weights learning during overtraining.
Grokking involves delayed generalization after memorization.
papers.limitation:
Coverage limitations remain significant across current methodologies.
Feature ontology challenges include poorly defined concepts of what constitutes a 'feature'.
future_direction: Developing a unified theory of developmental dynamics
Creating robust benchmarks and metrics for interpretability
Expanding interpretability to multimodal and agentic AI systems
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the nascent but critical field of developmental interpretability for Large Language Models. We chart the field's evolution from static, post-hoc analysis of trained models to a dynamic investigation of the training process itself. We begin by surveying the foundational methodologies, including representational probing, causal tracing, and circuit analysis, that enable researchers to deconstruct the learning process. The core of this review examines the developmental arc of LLM capabilities, detailing key findings on the formation and composition of computational circuits, the biphasic nature of knowledge acquisition, the transient dynamics of learning strategies like in-context learning, and the phenomenon of emergent abilities as phase transitions in training. We explore illuminating parallels with human cognitive and linguistic development, which provide valuable conceptual frameworks for understanding LLM learning. Finally, we argue that this developmental perspective is not merely an academic exercise but a cornerstone of proactive AI safety, offering a pathway to predict, monitor, and align the processes by which models acquire their capabilities. We conclude by outlining the grand challenges facing the field, such as scalability and automation, and propose a research agenda for building more transparent, reliable, and beneficial AI systems.

papers.title: Robustly Identifying Concepts Introduced During Chat Fine-Tuning Using Crosscoders
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether chat-only latents identified by crosscoders are genuinely unique to the fine-tuned model or if they are artifacts of the training loss, and how to robustly identify truly chat-specific concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two issues (Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling) in L1-trained crosscoders that cause false chat-only latent identification, proposes Latent Scaling to detect these issues, and demonstrates that BatchTopK crosscoders mitigate these issues and yield genuinely chat-specific and interpretable latents.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that using BatchTopK loss in crosscoders overcomes the limitations of L1 loss and provides a robust tool for model diffing, enabling concrete insights into how chat tuning modifies language model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The L1 crosscoder suffers from Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling, leading to many falsely identified chat-only latents.
Latent Scaling can detect these spurious chat-only latents by measuring how well they explain base model error and reconstruction.
BatchTopK crosscoders are robust to these issues and identify more genuinely chat-specific latents.
In BatchTopK crosscoders, the relative norm difference (Δnorm) is a meaningful metric for chat-specificity and causal importance, whereas in L1 crosscoders it is not.
The chat-specific latents found by BatchTopK crosscoders are highly interpretable and correspond to concepts like false information, personal questions, and various refusal triggers.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more layers and models.
Investigate the dynamics of concept emergence during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Model diffing is the study of how fine-tuning changes a model’s representations and internal algorithms. Many behaviours of interest are introduced during fine-tuning, and model diffing offers a promising lens to interpret such behaviors. Crosscoders[1] are a recent model diffing method that learns a shared dictionary of interpretable concepts represented as latent directions in both the base and fine-tuned models, allowing us to track how concepts shift or emerge during fine-tuning. Notably, prior work has observed concepts with no direction in the base model, and it was hypothesized that these model-specific latents were concepts introduced during fine-tuning. However, we identify two issues which stem from the crosscoders L1 training loss that can misattribute concepts as unique to the fine-tuned model, when they really exist in both models. We develop Latent Scaling to flag these issues by more accurately measuring each latent’s presence across models. In experiments comparing Gemma 2 2B base and chat models, we observe that the standard crosscoder suffers heavily from these issues. Building on these insights, we train a crosscoder with BatchTopK loss[2] and show that it substantially mitigates these issues, finding more genuinely chat-specific and highly interpretable concepts. We recommend practitioners adopt similar techniques. Using the BatchTopK crosscoder, we successfully identify a set of genuinely chat-specific latents that are both interpretable and causally effective, representing concepts such as _false information_ and _personal question_, along with multiple refusal-related latents that show nuanced preferences for different refusal triggers. Overall, our work advances best practices for the crosscoder-based methodology for model diffing and demonstrates that it can provide concrete insights into how chat tuning modifies language model behavior.1 Content Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful language.

papers.title: Convergent Linear Representations of Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms underlying emergent misalignment, and why does it generalize beyond the training domain?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that emergent misalignment is mediated by a convergent linear direction in activation space, and introduces a framework for interpreting rank-1 LoRA adapters, revealing that some adapters specialize for the fine-tuning domain while others contribute to general misalignment.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability can advance our understanding of emergent misalignment and that the identified convergent linear representation and LoRA analysis framework are steps towards monitoring and mitigating misalignment.
papers.key_findings:
A single direction in the residual stream can induce and ablate misalignment in the base model and in fine-tuned models.
This direction transfers across different fine-tuned models (trained with different datasets and LoRA configurations), indicating convergence in the representation of misalignment.
Some LoRA adapters specialize for misalignment in the fine-tuning domain (e.g., medicine), while others contribute to general misalignment.
The model exhibits self-correction behavior when steered towards misalignment, where it begins to discuss harmful topics but then corrects itself.
The misalignment direction extracted from activations and the direction from a single rank-1 LoRA adapter have low cosine similarity but converge downstream.
papers.limitation:
Insights are extracted from a small number of EM fine-tunes on a single model.
The use of LLM judges may decrease the reliability of results.
The evaluation questions are limited to 8 prompts, which may not encompass diverse and realistic deployment scenarios.
future_direction: Extracting and studying the directions already present in the chat model to understand how alignment-relevant concepts are represented.
Isolating the self-correction mechanism via circuit-based interpretability techniques.
Extending the LoRA vector analysis to understand the extent to which a dataset-relevant filter is learnt.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models on narrow datasets can cause them to develop broadly misaligned behaviours: a phenomena known as emergent misalignment. However, the mechanisms underlying this misalignment, and why it generalizes beyond the training domain, are poorly understood, demonstrating critical gaps in our knowledge of model alignment. In this work, we train and study a minimal model organism which uses just 9 rank-1 adapters to emergently misalign Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Studying this, we find that different emergently misaligned models converge to similar representations of misalignment. We demonstrate this convergence by extracting a 'misalignment direction' from one fine-tuned model's activations, and using it to effectively ablate misaligned behaviour from fine-tunes using higher dimensional LoRAs and different datasets. Leveraging the scalar hidden state of rank-1 LoRAs, we further present a set of experiments for directly interpreting the fine-tuning adapters, showing that six contribute to general misalignment, while two specialise for misalignment in just the fine-tuning domain. Emergent misalignment is a particularly salient example of undesirable and unexpected model behaviour and by advancing our understanding of the mechanisms behind it, we hope to move towards being able to better understand and mitigate misalignment more generally.

papers.title: LLM See, LLM Do: Guiding Data Generation to Target Non-Differentiable Objectives
papers.research_question: Can we explicitly steer models towards desired properties at test time by exploiting the synthetic data generation process, and what is the impact of passive inheritance of model properties via synthetic data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces active inheritance, a method to steer model behavior by targeted sampling of synthetic data to optimize non-differentiable objectives, and provides a comprehensive study of passive inheritance when models are trained on synthetic data.
papers.conclusion: Active inheritance is a promising and interpretable method for steering model behavior via synthetic data curation, enabling optimization of non-differentiable objectives without complex reinforcement learning or reward models.
papers.key_findings:
Models are sensitive to passive inheritance of properties from synthetic data, even when prompts are neutral.
Synthetic data can alter model preferences when used as evaluators, including alignment with human judgments and length bias.
Active inheritance can effectively steer model behavior, increasing desired attributes like length and lexical diversity and decreasing toxicity.
Multi-source sampling (using multiple teacher models) can enhance the effectiveness of active inheritance for some attributes.
The architecture prior of the base model remains a strong influence on preferences even after finetuning on synthetic data.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of synthetic data raises new questions about how models generating the data can influence other large language models (LLMs) via distilled data. To start, our work exhaustively characterizes the impact of passive inheritance of model properties by systematically studying the consequences of synthetic data integration. We provide one of the most comprehensive studies to-date of how the source of synthetic data shapes models' internal biases, calibration and generations' textual attributes and preferences. We find that models are surprisingly sensitive towards certain attributes even when the synthetic data prompts appear "neutral". which invites the question whether this sensitivity can be exploited for good. Our findings invite the question can we explicitly steer the models towards the properties we want at test time by exploiting the data generation process? This would have historically been considered infeasible due to the cost of collecting data with a specific characteristic or objective in mind. However, improvement in the quality of synthetic data, as well as a shift towards general-purpose models designed to follow a diverse way of instructions, means this question is timely. We propose active inheritance as a term to describe intentionally constraining synthetic data according to a non-differentiable objective. We demonstrate how active inheritance can steer the generation profiles of models towards desirable non-differentiable attributes, e.g. high lexical diversity or low toxicity.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: Unraveling the Influence of Training Data and Internal Structures in Large Language Models for Enhanced Explainability (Student Abstract)
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to estimate the influence of individual training data points in LLMs and how training data and internal components affect model performance across different usage modes and tasks.
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that influence functions combined with FAISS can efficiently identify influential training data points in LLMs, and that semantically related data points are crucial for model predictions.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that influence functions with FAISS can efficiently analyze training data influence in LLMs, and that semantically related data points are key to model predictions, providing a foundation for addressing issues like bias and hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
FAISS effectively identifies semantically influential training samples, whose removal decreases model accuracy.
Random removal of training data can improve accuracy by eliminating noisy samples.
TF-IDF-based sample removal does not significantly affect model performance.
Influence functions can be computed efficiently on subsets identified by FAISS for smaller models like GPT-2 Small.
LLM predictions are predominantly influenced by semantically related training points.
papers.limitation: Simpler models may not fully replicate complex LLMs, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more complex models and larger datasets.
Explore mechanistic interpretability to identify key internal components for specific tasks like machine translation and emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have expanded the application of large language models (LLMs) across fields such as medicine, finance, and education. Understanding the mechanisms underlying these models is essential to mitigate issues like hallucinations and bias. This study provides deep learning practitioners with insights into how specific training data points and internal structures influence model behaviour. Using influence functions and mechanistic interpretability, we will analyze the impact of data on model predictions across various tasks. Preliminary findings indicate that semantic search techniques, such as FAISS, enable efficient identification of influential training points in GPT-2 small. Future work will extend these methods to additional tasks and more complex models, with a focus on further elucidating LLM structures to improve interpretability.

papers.title: Patches of Nonlinearity: Instruction Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned language models internally process instructions, specifically how are instruction-specific representations constructed and utilized during post-training (SFT and DPO)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that instruction vectors (IVs) are localized, superadditive representations that act as circuit selectors, and introduces a novel method to analyze information flow without linear assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Instruction vectors are formed eagerly and act as circuit selectors, with their superadditive nature challenging existing linear assumptions in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Instruction vectors (IVs) are localized in the residual stream at the final instructional token.
IVs exhibit superadditivity: their combined causal influence is greater than the sum of individual influences.
IVs are linearly separable in representation space but interact non-linearly.
IVs act as circuit selectors, conditioning on task representations to select different information pathways in later layers.
Instruction tuning is necessary for IVs to acquire circuit-selection ability.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of instruction-tuned language models and their ubiquitous usage, very little is known of how models process instructions internally. In this work, we address this gap from a mechanistic point of view by investigating how instruction-specific representations are constructed and utilized in different stages of post-training: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Via causal mediation, we identify that instruction representation is fairly localized in models. These representations, which we call Instruction Vectors (IVs), demonstrate a curious juxtaposition of linear separability along with non-linear causal interaction, broadly questioning the scope of the linear representation hypothesis commonplace in mechanistic interpretability. To disentangle the non-linear causal interaction, we propose a novel method to localize information processing in language models that is free from the implicit linear assumptions of patching-based techniques. We find that, conditioned on the task representations formed in the early layers, different information pathways are selected in the later layers to solve that task, i.e., IVs act as circuit selectors.

papers.title: Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression: Intrinsic vs. Prompted Values in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences between intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in LLMs share common components for value expression but have unique elements that lead to differences in response diversity and steerability.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that while intrinsic and prompted mechanisms share commonalities, each possesses distinct components that serve different roles, clarifying when to prefer intrinsic versus prompted mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms exhibit nontrivial overlap at both the vector and neuron levels.
Shared components are crucial for value expression and generalize across languages, reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations.
Intrinsic-unique components promote lexical diversity in model responses.
Prompted-unique components strengthen instruction compliance and affect tasks like jailbreaking.
Value neurons can be decomposed into shared and unique types with distinct functional roles.
future_direction: Applying the analysis to AI safety applications such as diagnosing instruction-following behavior and improving robustness to undesirable behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models can express values in two main ways: (1) intrinsic expression, reflecting the model's inherent values learned during training, and (2) prompted expression, elicited by explicit prompts. Given their widespread use in value alignment, it is paramount to clearly understand their underlying mechanisms, particularly whether they mostly overlap (as one might expect) or rely on distinct mechanisms, but this remains largely understudied. We analyze this at the mechanistic level using two approaches: (1) value vectors, feature directions representing value mechanisms extracted from the residual stream, and (2) value neurons, MLP neurons that contribute to value vectors. We demonstrate that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms partly share common components crucial for inducing value expression, generalizing across languages and reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations in the model's internal representations. Yet, as these mechanisms also possess unique elements that fulfill distinct roles, they lead to different degrees of response diversity (intrinsic > prompted) and value steerability (prompted > intrinsic). In particular, components unique to the intrinsic mechanism promote lexical diversity in responses, whereas those specific to the prompted mechanism strengthen instruction following, taking effect even in distant tasks like jailbreaking.

papers.title: Cross-model Transferability among Large Language Models on the Platonic Representations of Concepts
papers.research_question: How can conceptual representations (steering vectors) be transferred across different large language models to enable cross-model behavioral control?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L-Cross Modulation, a linear transformation method to transfer steering vectors across LLMs, demonstrating that conceptual representations are linearly alignable and transferable, even from weaker to stronger models.
papers.conclusion: Cross-model transferability of conceptual representations is achievable via linear transformations, revealing a fundamental universality in how LLMs encode concepts, paving the way for more universal and adaptable language models.
papers.key_findings:
L-Cross Modulation effectively modulates target LLMs using steering vectors transferred from source LLMs.
The linear transformation matrix generalizes across different concepts, enabling alignment of SVs for multiple concepts.
Weak-to-strong transferability: SVs extracted from smaller LLMs can effectively modulate the behavior of larger LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The scope of concepts is limited to eleven benchmark concepts; creating more datasets is resource-intensive.
The evaluation metrics are diverse and may not generalize fully to all concepts.
The hyper-parameter (β) for applying steering vectors is manually tuned rather than automatically optimized.
future_direction: Expand to more high-level concepts with additional datasets.
Develop a unified, comprehensive evaluation framework including a standardized dataset and benchmark.
Automatically determine optimal hyperparameters for applying steering vectors.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical research frontier.
