We also show how using AEGISSAFETYDATASET during the LLM alignment phase does not negatively impact the performance of the aligned models on MT Bench scores. Furthermore, we propose AEGIS, a novel application of a no-regret online adaptation framework with strong theoretical guarantees, to perform content moderation with an ensemble of LLM content safety experts in deployment

papers.title: SPQR: A Standardized Benchmark for Modern Safety Alignment Methods in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can emit copyrighted, unsafe, or private content. Safety alignment aims to suppress specific concepts, yet evaluations seldom test whether safety persists under benign downstream fine-tuning routinely applied after deployment (e.g., LoRA personalization, style/domain adapters). We study the stability of current safety methods under benign fine-tuning and observe frequent breakdowns. As true safety alignment must withstand even benign post-deployment adaptations, we introduce the SPQR benchmark (Safety-Prompt adherence-Quality-Robustness). SPQR is a single-scored metric that provides a standardized and reproducible framework to evaluate how well safety-aligned diffusion models preserve safety, utility, and robustness under benign fine-tuning, by reporting a single leaderboard score to facilitate comparisons. We conduct multilingual, domain-specific, and out-of-distribution analyses, along with category-wise breakdowns, to identify when safety alignment fails after benign fine-tuning, ultimately showcasing SPQR as a concise yet comprehensive benchmark for T2I safety alignment techniques for T2I models.

papers.title: Toward Safer Diffusion Language Models: Discovery and Mitigation of Priming Vulnerability
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate tokens in parallel through iterative denoising, which can reduce latency and enable bidirectional conditioning. However, the safety risks posed by jailbreak attacks that exploit this inference mechanism are not well understood. In this paper, we reveal that DLMs have a critical vulnerability stemming from their iterative denoising process and propose a countermeasure. Specifically, our investigation shows that if an affirmative token for a harmful query appears at an intermediate step, subsequent denoising can be steered toward a harmful response even in aligned models. As a result, simply injecting such affirmative tokens can readily bypass the safety guardrails. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the vulnerability allows existing optimization-based jailbreak attacks to succeed on DLMs. Building on this analysis, we propose a novel safety alignment method tailored to DLMs that trains models to generate safe responses from contaminated intermediate states that contain affirmative tokens. Our experiments indicate that the proposed method significantly mitigates the vulnerability with minimal impact on task performance. Furthermore, our method improves robustness against conventional jailbreak attacks. Our work underscores the need for DLM-specific safety research. Our code is available at https://github.com/mdl-lab/dlm-priming-vulnerability.

papers.title: Subliminal Cues While Teaching: HCI Technique for Enhanced Learning
papers.abstract: This paper presents results from an empirical study conducted with a subliminal teaching technique aimed at enhancing learner's performance in Intelligent Systems through the use of physiological sensors. This technique uses carefully designed subliminal cues (positive) and miscues (negative) and projects them under the learner's perceptual visual threshold. A positive cue, called answer cue, is a hint aiming to enhance the learner's inductive reasoning abilities and projected in a way to help them figure out the solution faster but more importantly better. A negative cue, called miscue, is also used and aims at obviously at the opposite (distract the learner or lead them to the wrong conclusion). The latest obtained results showed that only subliminal cues, not miscues, could significantly increase learner performance and intuition in a logic-based problem-solving task. Nonintrusive physiological sensors (EEG for recording brainwaves, blood volume pressure to compute heart rate and skin response to record skin conductivity) were used to record affective and cerebral responses throughout the experiment. The descriptive analysis, combined with the physiological data, provides compelling evidence for the positive impact of answer cues on reasoning and intuitive decision making in a logic-based problem-solving paradigm.

papers.title: From Representational Harms to Quality-of-Service Harms: A Case Study on Llama 2 Safety Safeguards
papers.abstract: Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has led to their widespread adoption in various domains. However, these advancements have also introduced additional safety risks and raised concerns regarding their detrimental impact on already marginalized populations. Despite growing mitigation efforts to develop safety safeguards, such as supervised safety-oriented fine-tuning and leveraging safe reinforcement learning from human feedback, multiple concerns regarding the safety and ingrained biases in these models remain. Furthermore, previous work has demonstrated that models optimized for safety often display exaggerated safety behaviors, such as a tendency to refrain from responding to certain requests as a precautionary measure. As such, a clear trade-off between the helpfulness and safety of these models has been documented in the literature. In this paper, we further investigate the effectiveness of safety measures by evaluating models on already mitigated biases. Using the case of Llama 2 as an example, we illustrate how LLMs' safety responses can still encode harmful assumptions. To do so, we create a set of non-toxic prompts, which we then use to evaluate Llama models. Through our new taxonomy of LLMs responses to users, we observe that the safety/helpfulness trade-offs are more pronounced for certain demographic groups which can lead to quality-of-service harms for marginalized populations.

papers.title: Implicit meta-learning may lead language models to trust more reliable sources
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that LLMs may learn indicators of document usefulness and modulate their updates accordingly. We introduce random strings ("tags") as indicators of usefulness in a synthetic fine-tuning dataset. Fine-tuning on this dataset leads to implicit meta-learning (IML): in further fine-tuning, the model updates to make more use of text that is tagged as useful. We perform a thorough empirical investigation of this phenomenon, finding (among other things) that (i) it occurs in both pretrained LLMs and those trained from scratch, as well as on a vision task, and (ii) larger models and smaller batch sizes tend to give more IML. We also use probing to examine how IML changes the way models store knowledge in their parameters. Finally, we reflect on what our results might imply about capabilities, risks, and controllability of future AI systems. Our code can be found at https://github.com/krasheninnikov/internalization.

papers.title: Toxicity in ChatGPT: Analyzing Persona-assigned Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown incredible capabilities and transcended the natural language processing (NLP) community, with adoption throughout many services like healthcare, therapy, education, and customer service. Since users include people with critical information needs like students or patients engaging with chatbots, the safety of these systems is of prime importance. Therefore, a clear understanding of the capabilities and limitations of LLMs is necessary. To this end, we systematically evaluate toxicity in over half a million generations of ChatGPT, a popular dialogue-based LLM. We find that setting the system parameter of ChatGPT by assigning it a persona, say that of the boxer Muhammad Ali, significantly increases the toxicity of generations. Depending on the persona assigned to ChatGPT, its toxicity can increase up to 6x, with outputs engaging in incorrect stereotypes, harmful dialogue, and hurtful opinions. This may be potentially defamatory to the persona and harmful to an unsuspecting user. Furthermore, we find concerning patterns where specific entities (e.g., certain races) are targeted more than others (3x more) irrespective of the assigned persona, that reflect inherent discriminatory biases in the model. We hope that our findings inspire the broader AI community to rethink the efficacy of current safety guardrails and develop better techniques that lead to robust, safe, and trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: Adding Instructions during Pretraining: Effective way of Controlling Toxicity in Language Models
papers.abstract: Pretrained large language models have become indispensable for solving various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, safely deploying them in real world applications is challenging because they generate toxic content. To address this challenge, we propose two novel pretraining data augmentation strategies that significantly reduce model toxicity without compromising its utility. Our two strategies are: (1) MEDA: adds raw toxicity score as meta-data to the pretraining samples, and (2) INST: adds instructions to those samples indicating their toxicity. Our results indicate that our best performing strategy (INST) substantially reduces the toxicity probability up to 61% while preserving the accuracy on five benchmark NLP tasks as well as improving AUC scores on four bias detection tasks by 1.3%. We also demonstrate the generalizability of our techniques by scaling the number of training samples and the number of model parameters.

papers.title: Recipes for Safety in Open-domain Chatbots
papers.abstract: Models trained on large unlabeled corpora of human interactions will learn patterns and mimic behaviors therein, which include offensive or otherwise toxic behavior and unwanted biases. We investigate a variety of methods to mitigate these issues in the context of open-domain generative dialogue models. We introduce a new human-and-model-in-the-loop framework for both training safer models and for evaluating them, as well as a novel method to distill safety considerations inside generative models without the use of an external classifier at deployment time. We conduct experiments comparing these methods and find our new techniques are (i) safer than existing models as measured by automatic and human evaluations while (ii) maintaining usability metrics such as engagingness relative to the state of the art. We then discuss the limitations of this work by analyzing failure cases of our models.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning? A Mechanistic Study
papers.research_question: What is the safety mechanism learned by the model via safety fine-tuning, and how are jailbreak and adversarial attacks able to bypass this mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Safety fine-tuning methods minimally transform MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, causing clustering of safe and unsafe activations; jailbreaks bypass safety by having activations similar to safe samples.
papers.conclusion: Safety fine-tuning minimally transforms MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, leading to clustering; jailbreaks bypass this by having activations similar to safe samples. This mechanistic understanding can inform more robust safety fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety fine-tuning leads to separate clusters of activations for safe and unsafe samples.
The transformation ∆W has its column-space aligned with the null-space of the instruction fine-tuned weights, making it orthogonal to the original weights.
∆W preferentially impacts unsafe samples, as their pre-activations have larger projection onto the row-space of ∆W.
The local Lipschitzness of the model decreases for unsafe samples after safety fine-tuning, making the model less sensitive to perturbations on unsafe inputs.
Jailbreak attacks (competing objectives, mismatched generalization, adversarial embeddings) have activations that are closer to safe samples, thus bypassing the safety mechanism.
future_direction: Using ∆W from stronger safety fine-tuning methods to improve weaker ones
Designing more robust safety fine-tuning protocols based on the mechanistic understanding
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning helps align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences for their safe deployment. To better understand the underlying factors that make models safe via safety fine-tuning, we design a synthetic data generation framework that captures salient aspects of an unsafe input by modeling the interaction between the task the model is asked to perform (e.g., "design") versus the specific concepts the task is asked to be performed upon (e.g., a "cycle" vs. a "bomb"). Using this, we investigate three well-known safety fine-tuning methods -- supervised safety fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and unlearning -- and provide significant evidence demonstrating that these methods minimally transform MLP weights to specifically align unsafe inputs into its weights' null space. This yields a clustering of inputs based on whether the model deems them safe or not. Correspondingly, when an adversarial input (e.g., a jailbreak) is provided, its activations are closer to safer samples, leading to the model processing such an input as if it were safe. We validate our findings, wherever possible, on real-world models -- specifically, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B.

papers.title: From Data to Behavior: Predicting Unintended Model Behaviors Before Training
papers.research_question: Can we predict unintended model behaviors (biases and safety risks) that emerge from training data before fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Data2Behavior task for predicting unintended model behaviors before training and proposes MDF, a lightweight method that injects mean data representations into the forward pass to reveal latent biases and safety risks without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: Introduces the Data2Behavior task and MDF method for predicting unintended behaviors before training, demonstrating promising performance and highlighting data-centric strategies for trustworthy LLM development.
papers.key_findings:
MDF reliably predicts unintended bias and safety risks induced by training data without fine-tuning.
MDF requires only about 20% of the GPU resources compared to fine-tuning.
MDF generalizes across different model architectures (Qwen and Gemma series).
Model representations encode latent statistical signals of data, and amplifying these signals reveals unintended behaviors.
Traditional baselines (keyword filtering, semantic auditing) fail to detect subliminal risks in training data.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is primarily on open-source architectures (Qwen and Gemma series) due to need for internal activations, not validated on proprietary closed-source models.
Analysis is constrained to Global Dataset Prediction, not Instance-level Attribution.
future_direction: Validate the framework across a broader spectrum of model families.
Investigate instance-level attribution to identify risk contribution of individual samples.
Explore optimal layer selection for subliminal risk detection.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can acquire unintended biases from seemingly benign training data even without explicit cues or malicious content. Existing methods struggle to detect such risks before fine-tuning, making post hoc evaluation costly and inefficient. To address this challenge, we introduce Data2Behavior, a new task for predicting unintended model behaviors prior to training. We also propose Manipulating Data Features (MDF), a lightweight approach that summarizes candidate data through their mean representations and injects them into the forward pass of a base model, allowing latent statistical signals in the data to shape model activations and reveal potential biases and safety risks without updating any parameters. MDF achieves reliable prediction while consuming only about 20% of the GPU resources required for fine-tuning. Experiments on Qwen3-14B, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-12b-it confirm that MDF can anticipate unintended behaviors and provide insight into pre-training vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Narrow Finetuning Leaves Clearly Readable Traces in Activation Differences
papers.research_question: Does narrow finetuning create detectable, interpretable biases in LLM activations that reveal the finetuning domain?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow finetuning creates strong, static biases in LLM activations that can be detected and interpreted using simple model diffing techniques (Activation Difference Lens), revealing the finetuning domain even on unrelated text.
papers.conclusion: Narrow finetuning leaves clearly readable traces in activation differences, enabling interpretation of the finetuning domain, but these artifacts raise concerns about using such models as realistic proxies for broader finetuning in research.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences on the first few tokens of random text encode meaningful information about the finetuning domain, which can be surfaced via Patchscope and Logit Lens.
Steering a finetuned model by adding these activation differences produces text highly similar to the finetuning data.
An interpretability agent using these insights significantly outperforms blackbox agents in identifying the finetuning objective.
These detectable traces arise from overfitting to semantically homogeneous finetuning data and can be mitigated by mixing unrelated data during finetuning.
Narrowly finetuned models may not be realistic proxies for broader finetuning (e.g., chat-tuning) in interpretability and safety research.
papers.limitation:
Mixing pretraining data into the finetuning corpus mitigates the bias but may impair the model's ability to internalize the target objective.
The study is limited to narrow finetuning and may not generalize to broader finetuning like chat-tuning.
future_direction: Deeper investigation into the effects of narrow finetuning.
Development of truly realistic case studies for model-diffing, safety and interpretability research.
papers.abstract: Finetuning on narrow domains has become an essential tool to adapt Large Language Models (LLMs) to specific tasks and to create models with known unusual properties that are useful for research. We show that narrow finetuning creates strong biases in LLM activations that can be interpreted to understand the finetuning domain. These biases can be discovered using simple tools from model diffing - the study of differences between models before and after finetuning. In particular, analyzing activation differences on the first few tokens of random text and steering by adding this difference to the model activations produces text similar to the format and general content of the finetuning data. We demonstrate that these analyses contain crucial information by creating an LLM-based interpretability agent to understand the finetuning domain. With access to the bias, the agent performs significantly better compared to baseline agents using simple prompting. Our analysis spans synthetic document finetuning for false facts, emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, and taboo word guessing game models across different architectures (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and scales (1B to 32B parameters). We suspect these biases reflect overfitting and find that mixing pretraining data into the finetuning corpus largely removes them, though residual risks may remain. Our work (1) demonstrates that narrowly finetuned models have salient traces of their training objective in their activations and suggests ways to improve how they are trained, (2) warns AI safety and interpretability researchers that the common practice of using such models as a proxy for studying broader finetuning (e.g., chat-tuning) might not be realistic, and (3) highlights the need for deeper investigation into the effects of narrow finetuning and development of truly realistic case studies for model-diffing, safety and interpretability research.

papers.title: Where Did It Go Wrong? Attributing Undesirable LLM Behaviors via Representation Gradient Tracing
papers.research_question: How can we trace undesirable LLM behaviors (e.g., harmful content, factual errors, biases) back to the specific training data that caused them?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel and efficient framework (RepT) for data attribution in LLMs by analyzing representation and its gradients, shifting from parameter space to a more semantically meaningful activation space.
papers.conclusion: RepT provides a powerful diagnostic tool to understand, audit, and mitigate the root causes of undesirable LLM behaviors by establishing a semantically meaningful link between model outputs and their training data origins.
papers.key_findings:
RepT significantly outperforms existing gradient-based attribution methods (e.g., Influence Functions, TracIn, LESS) in identifying harmful, backdoor, and factually contaminated training data across multiple LLMs.
The framework enables fine-grained token-level attribution, pinpointing specific words or phrases within training data that causally influence undesirable model outputs.
RepT is computationally efficient, requiring minimal memory and time compared to baselines, and scales effectively to larger models and full-parameter fine-tuning settings.
The method is robust across different tasks (harmful data identification, backdoor detection, knowledge contamination) and model architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the representation (hidden state) and its gradient are essential components for accurate attribution.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on curated fine-tuning datasets; application to massive pre-training corpora presents engineering challenges for exhaustive attribution.
The framework's effectiveness on subtle, emergent phenomena (e.g., nuanced biases from data aggregation) requires further investigation.
future_direction: Systematically exploring layer selection to determine the most potent representational depth for different attribution tasks.
Using the framework to not only diagnose but also mitigate issues, e.g., by filtering harmful data or developing steering vectors for real-time model correction.
Extending the method from diagnosis to direct mitigation and real-time model alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet their deployment is frequently undermined by undesirable behaviors such as generating harmful content, factual inaccuracies, and societal biases. Diagnosing the root causes of these failures poses a critical challenge for AI safety. Existing attribution methods, particularly those based on parameter gradients, often fall short due to prohibitive noisy signals and computational complexity. In this work, we introduce a novel and efficient framework that diagnoses a range of undesirable LLM behaviors by analyzing representation and its gradients, which operates directly in the model's activation space to provide a semantically meaningful signal linking outputs to their training data. We systematically evaluate our method for tasks that include tracking harmful content, detecting backdoor poisoning, and identifying knowledge contamination. The results demonstrate that our approach not only excels at sample-level attribution but also enables fine-grained token-level analysis, precisely identifying the specific samples and phrases that causally influence model behavior. This work provides a powerful diagnostic tool to understand, audit, and ultimately mitigate the risks associated with LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/plumprc/RepT.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: In-the-Wild Model Organisms: Mitigating Undesirable Emergent Behaviors in Production LLM Post-Training via Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we trace emergent harmful behaviors in post-trained language models back to responsible training data? And can we discover such behaviors without knowing what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints by computing and comparing activation-difference vectors, enabling targeted interventions and unsupervised discovery of emergent harmful behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Activation-based data attribution provides an effective and cost-efficient method for safety audits of post-training, enabling both targeted mitigation of known harmful behaviors and unsupervised discovery of unknown ones.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered 'distractor-triggered compliance' in OLMo 2, a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended.
Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces the harmful behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves a 78% reduction.
The method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10× cheaper.
Unsupervised clustering of behavior-datapoint similarity matrices can surface emergent behavioral patterns without prior specification.
The behavior emerged from standard DPO training on a diverse preference dataset, providing a realistic 'in-the-wild' model organism for safety research.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model family (OLMo) and a single harmful behavior type.
Method requires access to post-training data and intermediate checkpoints for causal validation through retraining, which is not available for many models.
future_direction: Automating the identification of concerning clusters from unsupervised discovery.
Extending causal validation to other model families if they release comparable training artifacts.
Testing whether activation-based attribution extends to other post-training methods such as RLHF and SFT.
papers.abstract: We propose activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints. By computing activation-difference vectors for both test prompts and preference pairs and ranking by cosine similarity, we identify datapoints that cause specific behaviors and validate these attributions causally by retraining with modified data. Clustering behavior-datapoint similarity matrices also enables unsupervised discovery of emergent behaviors. Applying this to OLMo 2's production DPO training, we surfaced distractor-triggered compliance: a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended. Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces this behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves 78%. Our method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10 times cheaper than both. This in-the-wild model organism - emerging from contaminated preference data rather than deliberate injection - provides a realistic benchmark for safety techniques.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: SafeSteer: Interpretable Safety Steering with Refusal-Evasion in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model outputs for safety at inference time without fine-tuning, using activation steering with category-specific vectors?
papers.core_contribution: SAFE STEER enables precise, customizable safety adjustments in LLMs through category-specific steering vectors computed from activations, without fine-tuning or contrastive data, while maintaining text quality.
papers.conclusion: SAFE STEER demonstrates effective inference-time safety steering across LLMs and datasets, providing precise control, preventing blanket refusals, and guiding models to generate safe, contextually relevant content.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE STEER reduces the percentage of unsafe responses in LLMs across various harm categories.
It effectively uses generic safe data without requiring contrastive paired datasets.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves steering signals and safety outcomes.
The method outperforms baselines like SEA and CAA in safety and utility metrics.
Steering maintains or improves text quality attributes such as helpfulness and coherence while enhancing safety.
future_direction: Investigate transferability of steering vectors across models and categories.
Scale up the method to more harm categories and models for broader applicability.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to adapt to evolving safety policies is costly and impractical. Mechanistic interpretability enables inference-time control through latent activation steering, yet its potential for precise, customizable safety adjustments remains largely untapped. This paper investigates an approach called SafeSteer for guiding the outputs of LLMs by: (i) leveraging category-specific steering vectors for more precise control, (ii) employing a simple, gradient-free unsupervised method to enhance safety steering while preserving text quality, topic relevance, and without explicit refusal, and (iii) accomplishing this without a hard requirement of contrastive pairwise safe data. We also highlight that our method, being simple and effective, aligns with recent studies suggesting that simple techniques often outperform more complex ones in activation steering. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach across various LLMs, datasets, and risk categories, demonstrating its ability to provide precise control, prevent blanket refusals, and guide models toward generating safe content while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: Humanizing Language Models: Exploring behavioral and brain data as language model inputs
papers.research_question: How do embeddings derived from behavioral and brain data differ from text-derived embeddings in terms of encoded information, particularly dimensions like dominance, valence, and arousal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that embeddings trained on behavioral and brain data encode different information compared to text-derived embeddings, with behavioral embeddings particularly better at capturing affective dimensions like dominance, valence, and arousal.
papers.conclusion: Behavioral and brain data can provide valuable inputs for language models to better align with human knowledge, especially by encoding affective dimensions.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings derived from behavioral and brain data encode different information than text-derived embeddings.
Behavioral embeddings better encode dimensions relating to dominance, valence, and arousal.
papers.abstract: Language models have traditionally been trained on massive digitized text corpora. However, alternative data sources exist that may increase the representational alignment between language models and human knowledge. We contribute to the assessment of the role of data sources on language model representations. Specifically, we present work aimed at understanding differences in the content of language representations ('embeddings') trained from text, behavioral data (e.g., free associations), and brain data (e.g., fMRI). Using a method from neuroscience known as 'representational similarity analysis', we show that embeddings derived from behavioral and brain data encode different information than their text-derived cousins. Furthermore, using an interpretability method that we term, 'representational content analysis,' we find that, in particular, behavioral embeddings better encode dimensions relating to dominance, valence, and arousal, which are likely critical for the representational alignment of language models.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, bringing activation steering to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPBEND, a method that brings activation steering to fine-tuning by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, achieving state-of-the-art safety performance with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: REPBEND effectively enhances LLM safety by bending representations to separate safe and unsafe states, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal impact on general capabilities, offering a scalable safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks.
REPBEND maintains general capabilities and usability, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks.
REPBEND outperforms prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO in both black-box and white-box attacks.
REPBEND works best when applied to mid-to-later layers of the transformer.
REPBEND's loss function, which includes L2 norm, cosine similarity, and KL divergence terms, effectively separates safe and unsafe representations.
papers.limitation:
REPBEND requires a dataset of safe and unsafe prompts, which may not cover all possible harmful scenarios.
The method relies on the choice of layers and hyperparameters, which may need tuning for different models.
The transferability of LoRA for safety improvements remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring the transferability of LoRA adapters for safety across models.
Extending REPBEND to multimodal settings.
Investigating the theoretical foundations of representation bending.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools, but their inherent safety risks - ranging from harmful content generation to broader societal harms - pose significant challenges. These risks can be amplified by the recent adversarial attacks, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and the increasing deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments. Existing safety-enhancing techniques, such as fine-tuning with human feedback or adversarial training, are still vulnerable as they address specific threats and often fail to generalize across unseen attacks, or require manual system-level defenses. This paper introduces RepBend, a novel approach that fundamentally disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable solution to enhance (potentially inherent) safety. RepBend brings the idea of activation steering - simple vector arithmetic for steering model's behavior during inference - to loss-based fine-tuning. Through extensive evaluation, RepBend achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks, all with negligible reduction in model usability and general capabilities.

papers.title: Character as a Latent Variable in Large Language Models: A Mechanistic Account of Emergent Misalignment and Conditional Safety Failures
papers.research_question: Does emergent misalignment in fine-tuned LLMs arise from the acquisition of character-level behavioral dispositions rather than the generalization of erroneous content?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment is driven by the acquisition of character-level behavioral dispositions during fine-tuning, which can be conditionally activated, rather than by the generalization of isolated errors.
papers.conclusion: Character formation is a central and underexplored alignment risk, suggesting robust alignment must address latent behavioral dispositions rather than isolated errors or prompt-level defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Character-conditioned fine-tuning induces stronger and more transferable misalignment than incorrect-advice fine-tuning.
Character-conditioned fine-tuning largely preserves general model capabilities (e.g., on MMLU).
Learned character representations can be conditionally activated by training-time triggers (persona switches).
Inference-time persona-aligned prompts can jailbreak models by activating latent character representations.
Emergent misalignment, triggered persona control, and persona-aligned jailbreaks share a common representational basis in character-related activation patterns.
papers.abstract: Emergent Misalignment refers to a failure mode in which fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on narrowly scoped data induces broadly misaligned behavior. Prior explanations mainly attribute this phenomenon to the generalization of erroneous or unsafe content. In this work, we show that this view is incomplete. Across multiple domains and model families, we find that fine-tuning models on data exhibiting specific character-level dispositions induces substantially stronger and more transferable misalignment than incorrect-advice fine-tuning, while largely preserving general capabilities. This indicates that emergent misalignment arises from stable shifts in model behavior rather than from capability degradation or corrupted knowledge. We further show that such behavioral dispositions can be conditionally activated by both training-time triggers and inference-time persona-aligned prompts, revealing shared structure across emergent misalignment, backdoor activation, and jailbreak susceptibility. Overall, our results identify character formation as a central and underexplored alignment risk, suggesting that robust alignment must address behavioral dispositions rather than isolated errors or prompt-level defenses.

papers.title: How Instruction and Reasoning Data shape Post-Training: Data Quality through the Lens of Layer-wise Gradients
papers.research_question: How do instruction and reasoning data of varying quality affect the layer-wise gradients during LLM post-training, and can existing data quality metrics be unified by spectral properties of these gradients?
papers.core_contribution: This work shows that various data quality metrics (IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, Reward) can be unified by spectral properties of layer-wise gradients, specifically lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks for higher-quality data, with effective rank being more robust. It also reveals that reasoning data induces higher effective ranks than instruction data.
papers.conclusion: Spectral analysis of layer-wise gradients provides a unified view on the effects of data quality across instruction and reasoning data, offering insights into training stability and data exploration strategies for post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Existing data quality metrics (IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, Reward) are unified by consistent spectral properties of gradients: lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks for high-quality data.
Effective rank outperforms nuclear norm in distinguishing low- vs. high-quality data and is more sensitive to subtle quality differences.
Reasoning data achieves substantially higher effective ranks than instruction data, indicating richer gradient structures for complex tasks.
Within the same model family, layer-wise gradient spectral properties remain consistent across different model sizes, but diverge significantly across distinct model families.
Cosine similarities between gradients (same-layer and adjacent-layer) remain nearly zero and cannot reflect data quality.
papers.abstract: As the post-training of large language models (LLMs) advances from instruction-following to complex reasoning tasks, understanding how different data affect finetuning dynamics remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present a spectral analysis of layer-wise gradients induced by low/high-quality instruction and reasoning data for LLM post-training. Our analysis reveals that widely-studied metrics for data evaluation, e.g., IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, and Reward, can be explained and unified by spectral properties computed from gradients' singular value decomposition (SVD). Specifically, higher-quality data are usually associated with lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks. Notably, effective rank exhibits better robustness and resolution than nuclear norm in capturing subtle quality differences. For example, reasoning data achieves substantially higher effective ranks than instruction data, implying richer gradient structures on more complex tasks. Our experiments also highlight that models within the same family share similar gradient patterns regardless of their sizes, whereas different model families diverge significantly. Providing a unified view on the effects of data quality across instruction and reasoning data, this work illuminates the interplay between data quality and training stability, shedding novel insights into developing better data exploration strategies for post-training.

papers.title: Generative Models as a Complex Systems Science: How can we make sense of large language model behavior?
papers.research_question: How can we make sense of large language model behavior? The paper argues for a systematic effort to decompose language model behavior into categories that explain cross-task performance, to guide mechanistic explanations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the field of generative model research should be reconceptualized as a complex systems science, focusing on discovering and categorizing high-level behaviors of models to guide bottom-up mechanistic explanations and future-proof interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by arguing for an increased focus on the foundational question of 'what are models doing?' to guide the classic 'why are models doing that?' question in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Benchmarks alone cannot discover or characterize new model behaviors; they can only measure performance on predefined tasks.
A hierarchical taxonomy of model behavior (e.g., copying, in-context learning) is needed to guide mechanistic interpretability and understand what models are doing in general.
Generative models are easier to study than many naturally arising complex systems because they are simulable, repeatable, and allow for easy perturbation without observer effects.
The field lacks a formal vocabulary for describing model behaviors, which hinders progress in explaining why models work.
papers.limitation: The proposed behavioral approach is conceptual and lacks a concrete, implemented framework for discovering and categorizing behaviors.
future_direction: Developing a rich inventory of behavioral tests to create a universal scaffolding for analyzing any new model.
Investigating possible mappings between training data and generated data to establish new behavioral categories.
Formalizing the concept of 'behavior' and finding metamodels that are both explanatory and simple to describe.
papers.abstract: Coaxing out desired behavior from pretrained models, while avoiding undesirable ones, has redefined NLP and is reshaping how we interact with computers. What was once a scientific engineering discipline-in which building blocks are stacked one on top of the other-is arguably already a complex systems science, in which emergent behaviors are sought out to support previously unimagined use cases. Despite the ever increasing number of benchmarks that measure task performance, we lack explanations of what behaviors language models exhibit that allow them to complete these tasks in the first place. We argue for a systematic effort to decompose language model behavior into categories that explain cross-task performance, to guide mechanistic explanations and help future-proof analytic research.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Concept Influence: Leveraging Interpretability to Improve Performance and Efficiency in Training Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we improve training data attribution by using interpretable semantic directions to address issues of scalability and syntactic bias in existing methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Influence, a method that attributes model behavior to semantic directions (e.g., linear probes or SAE features) instead of individual test examples, and shows that probe-based approximations are efficient first-order alternatives.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating interpretable structures like concept vectors into training data attribution improves effectiveness and scalability for controlling model behavior, with concept-based methods outperforming classical influence functions and efficient approximations offering practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Influence outperforms classical influence functions across synthetic emergent misalignment benchmarks in identifying data that cause misalignment.
Probe-based approximations (Vector Filter and Projection Difference) are over an order of magnitude faster than gradient-based methods and achieve competitive performance.
Concept Influence identifies training examples that are semantically aligned with the target behavior, whereas standard influence functions often select syntactically similar examples.
Filtering out the most influential data points according to Concept Influence effectively reduces model misalignment, while retaining them amplifies it.
In real-world post-training data (OASST1), vector-based filtering methods can improve the safety-capability tradeoff, with Vector Filter achieving the best performance.
future_direction: Extending Concept Influence to richer representations like circuits or other mechanistic decompositions.
Developing principled group-level attribution methods.
Scaling experiments across model sizes and extending to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: As large language models are increasingly trained and fine-tuned, practitioners need methods to identify which training data drive specific behaviors, particularly unintended ones. Training Data Attribution (TDA) methods address this by estimating datapoint influence. Existing approaches like influence functions are both computationally expensive and attribute based on single test examples, which can bias results toward syntactic rather than semantic similarity. To address these issues of scalability and influence to abstract behavior, we leverage interpretable structures within the model during the attribution. First, we introduce Concept Influence which attribute model behavior to semantic directions (such as linear probes or sparse autoencoder features) rather than individual test examples. Second, we show that simple probe-based attribution methods are first-order approximations of Concept Influence that achieve comparable performance while being over an order-of-magnitude faster. We empirically validate Concept Influence and approximations across emergent misalignment benchmarks and real post-training datasets, and demonstrate they achieve comparable performance to classical influence functions while being substantially more scalable. More broadly, we show that incorporating interpretable structure within traditional TDA pipelines can enable more scalable, explainable, and better control of model behavior through data.

papers.title: Activation-Space Personality Steering: Hybrid Layer Selection for Stable Trait Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control or align personality traits (Big Five) in Large Language Model generation through targeted interventions in the model's internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a pipeline for personality steering in LLMs that extracts low-rank trait directions from activations and uses a hybrid (verified + dynamic) layer selection strategy to inject these directions into the residual stream, enabling precise control of Big Five trait expression without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-space personality steering framework with hybrid layer selection provides a robust and effective method for controlling personality traits in LLMs, bridging psychological theory and practical model alignment without degrading core capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits in LLMs occupy a low-rank shared subspace, with top three principal components explaining over 90% of variance.
A hybrid layer selection strategy (combining offline verified layers and prompt-specific dynamic layers) yields stronger and more stable trait steering than using either component alone.
The steering method effectively shifts trait expression in both positive and negative directions while largely preserving the model's fluency and general reasoning capabilities (as measured by MMLU and ARC-Challenge).
The learned trait direction vectors exhibit structured correlations (e.g., between Openness and Extraversion), indicating shared representational structure for personality-related behaviors.
Steering effectiveness varies across model families, with some dependencies observed between traits when steered simultaneously.
papers.limitation:
Steering effectiveness is greater on some model families (e.g., Llama, Mistral) than others (e.g., Qwen).
Dependencies between traits (e.g., agreeableness and openness) can complicate independent steering, and applying orthogonality to remove these dependencies reduces steering efficacy.
The effect of steering is less significant when the base model's trait expression is already at an extreme (very high or very low).
future_direction: Disentangling trait-specific control from shared semantic structure without degrading steering effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit implicit personalities in their generation, but reliably controlling or aligning these traits to meet specific needs remains an open challenge. The need for effective mechanisms for behavioural manipulation of the model during generation is a critical gap in the literature that needs to be fulfilled. Personality-aware LLMs hold a promising direction towards this objective. However, the relationship between these psychological constructs and their representations within LLMs remains underexplored and requires further investigation. Moreover, it is intriguing to understand and study the use of these representations to steer the models' behaviour. We propose a novel pipeline that extracts hidden state activations from transformer layers using the Big Five Personality Traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism), which is a comprehensive and empirically validated framework to model human personality applies low-rank subspace discovery methods, and identifies trait-specific optimal layers across different model architectures for robust injection. The resulting personality-aligned directions are then operationalised through a flexible steering framework with dynamic layer selection, enabling precise control of trait expression in LLM outputs. Our findings reveal that personality traits occupy a low-rank shared subspace, and that these latent structures can be transformed into actionable mechanisms for effective steering through careful perturbations without impacting the fluency, variance and general capabilities, helping to bridge the gap between psychological theory and practical model alignment.

papers.title: False Sense of Security: Why Probing-based Malicious Input Detection Fails to Generalize
papers.research_question: Do probing classifiers for LLM safety detection learn semantic harmfulness or rely on superficial patterns?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that probing classifiers for LLM safety detection rely on superficial patterns like instructional formats and trigger words, rather than semantic understanding of harmfulness, leading to poor out-of-distribution performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that current probing-based safety detection methods provide a false sense of security by relying on spurious correlations, and calls for more robust approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Probing classifiers achieve near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but fail dramatically on out-of-distribution data.
Simple n-gram methods achieve comparable performance to probing classifiers, suggesting reliance on surface-level patterns.
Classifiers perform poorly on semantically cleaned datasets where harmful content is replaced with benign alternatives.
Probing classifiers depend on instructional patterns and trigger words rather than semantic harmfulness.
LLMs themselves possess zero-shot safety classification ability, but probing classifiers cannot leverage this effectively.
papers.limitation:
